signals.title: [Bug]: OAuth2 client_credentials MCP servers never receive client_id/client_secret at runtime — token endpoint always rejects with 400
signals.text: ### What happened? Registering an MCP server with `auth_type: oauth2` / `oauth2_flow: client_credentials` results in `tools/list` failing 100% of the time with: ``` misconfigured: OAuth2 client_credentials grant rejected: token endpoint returned HTTP 400 ``` This happens **regardless of how the server is configured** — via the REST API (`POST /v1/mcp/server` with a nested `credentials: {client_id, client_secret}` object) or via `config.yaml`'s `mcp_servers:` block (with either `os.environ/VAR` or literal values). In every case the token endpoint (a real, independently-verified-working Keycloak `client_credentials` grant) rejects the request, which points to litellm sending an empty or malformed `client_id`/`client_secret`. ### Root cause (traced in source, not guessed) 1. **`LiteLLM_MCPServerTable` (`schema.prisma`) has no `client_id` / `client_secret` columns** — only an encrypted `credentials Json?` blob: ```prisma model LiteLLM_MCPServerTable { server_id String @id @default(uuid()) ... credentials Json? @default("{}") ... } ``` 2. The runtime OAuth2 resolver builds its config from **flat fields on the `MCPServer` Pydantic model**: `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/outbound_credentials/adapter.py`: ```python config=ClientCredentialsConfig( client_id=server.client_id, client_secret=SecretStr(server.client_secret) if server.client_secret else None, token_url=server.token_url, ... ) ``` 3. **Nothing in the codebase ever copies the decrypted `credentials` blob into `server.client_id` / `server.client_secret`.** Searched the whole `mcp_server` package for any `client_id=<decrypted value>` assignment feeding into an `MCPServer(...)` construction used by the OAuth2 resolver — there is none. `decrypt_credentials()` is only used for master-key rotation (`rotate_mcp_server_credentials_master_key`) and DCR client storage, never to populate the resolver's config. Result: for any server persisted through the database (which is every server registered via the REST API, and — because `general_settings.store_model_in_db: true` is a very common production setting — effectively every `config.yaml`-defined server too), `server.client_id` / `server.client_secret` are **always `None`** at the point the token request is built. Keycloak (or any spec-compliant IdP) correctly returns `400 invalid_request`/`invalid_client` for a `client_credentials` grant with an empty `client_id`. 4. Separately, **`config.yaml`'s `mcp_servers:` loader does not resolve `os.environ/VAR`** for `client_id`/`client_secret`, unlike `model_list.litellm_params`: `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py`: ```python client_id=server_config.get("client_id", None), client_secret=server_config.get("client_secret", None), ``` This is a plain dict `.get()` — no `get_secret()` / env-var indirection. The [MCP OAuth docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/mcp_oauth) show `client_id: os.environ/MCP_CLIENT_ID` as the documented pattern, but it is silently taken as a literal string, so the literal text `os.environ/MCP_CLIENT_ID` gets sent to the token endpoint instead of the resolved secret. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Register (via REST API or `config.yaml`) an MCP server: ```yaml mcp_servers: my_server: url: "https://my-mcp-server.example.com/mcp" transport: http auth_type: oauth2 oauth2_flow: client_credentials client_id: "<a real, working client_id>" client_secret: "<its real secret>" token_url: "https://idp.example.com/protocol/openid-connect/token" ``` 2. Independently confirm the same `client_id`/`client_secret`/`token_url` succeed with a plain `curl -d grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=...&client_secret=...` — they do (200, valid token). 3. Call `tools/list` against the proxy's `/mcp/` endpoint for this server. 4. Observe `"status": "internal", "http_status": 500"` in `_meta.litellm.ai/server_outcomes`, and in the proxy logs: ``` Failed to get tools from server my_server: 500: misconfigured: OAuth2 client_credentials grant rejected: token endpoint returned HTTP 400 ``` 5. Confirm the grant mechanics themselves are fine by calling litellm's own `_prepare_grant` / `post_client_credentials_grant` directly with the identical config object (bypassing the server-record load path) — this **succeeds** and returns a valid access token. The bug is specifically in how the persisted/config-loaded `MCPServer` record's credentials reach that function, not in the grant logic itself. ### Expected behavior `client_id`/`client_secret` provided at registration time (via API `credentials` object or `config.yaml`, with or without `os.environ/` indirection) should reach the actual token request unchanged. ### Suggested fix - Add `client_id`/`client_secret` columns to `LiteLLM_MCPServerTable` (or decrypt+unpack the `credentials` blob into the `MCPServer.client_id`/`client_secret` fields at every read path that feeds `_client_credentials_spec`), and/or - Apply the same `get_secret()`/`os.environ/` resolution used for `model_list` to the `mcp_servers:` config.yaml loader for `client_id`, `client_secret`, and any other credential-shaped field. ### Environment - **LiteLLM version**: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, image pulled/deployed 2026-08-10 (prod) — well after the March 2026 fix for #24522, so this is not that issue. - **What part of LiteLLM is this about?**: MCP Gateway / OAuth2 `client_credentials` - Reproduced independently on two separate deployments (Azure Container Apps and an OpenShift-hosted instance with `store_model_in_db: true`), both via REST API registration and via `config.yaml`. ### Related issues Not a duplicate of #24522 (concurrent stateless teardown — different traceback, different mechanism). Possibly related in spirit to #22755 ("Unable to list MCP tools with OAuth through the UI Dashboard", closed `not_planned`) and #15957, which describe the same outward symptom (OAuth-protected MCP tool listing fails) without this root cause having been identified. --- ## Bug 2: `true_passthrough`/`oauth_delegate` MCP sessions time out despite the upstream call itself completing in milliseconds ### What happened? As an alternative to `client_credentials` (see Bug 1), we tested `auth_type: oauth_delegate` (`true_passthrough`), where litellm is supposed to forward the caller's own bearer token verbatim (via the `x-mcp-{alias}-authorization` header) instead of minting its own. `tools/list` against this server times out inside litellm. ### Root cause (traced in source) - `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/outbound_credentials/resolver.py`, `_passthrough(self, subject)` (~line 163) forwards `subject.inbound_token` verbatim to the upstream MCP server — this part is correct and matches the caller-supplied-credential design we wanted. - `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py` (~line 4200) wraps the actual `client.list_tools()` call in `anyio.fail_after(MCP_TOOL_LISTING_TIMEOUT)`. In our reproduction, this consistently fires before the upstream ever responds. - We isolated the upstream call from litellm's session/connection handling entirely: a standalone script (`debug_passthrough.py`), running inside the same cluster network as litellm and using the same caller token forwarded the same way, hit the internal MCP URL directly and got back **`HTTP 200` in `0.04s`**. The upstream server, network path, and token are all fine — the timeout is happening somewhere in litellm's own MCP client/session plumbing between accepting the passthrough token and actually completing the `list_tools()` round trip. ### Expected behavior `tools/list` over a `true_passthrough`/`oauth_delegate` MCP server should complete in roughly the same time as a direct call to the upstream (tens of milliseconds in our environment), not hit `MCP_TOOL_LISTING_TIMEOUT`. ### Environment Same as Bug 1 (OpenShift-hosted litellm instance, `store_model_in_db: true`). ### Status This is reported with less certainty than Bug 1 — we have not yet traced the exact point inside litellm's session/connection setup where the delay is introduced (as opposed to Bug 1, which we traced to an exact missing assignment). Flagging it here because it blocks the architecturally-preferred alternative to Bug 1. --- ## Bug 3: `client_credentials` grant requests every scope advertised by the realm's discovery document, instead of only the client's assigned scopes ### What happened? With Bug 1's root cause fixed locally (server record correctly populated with a real, independently-verified-working `client_id`/`client_secret`), the *live* litellm instance's `client_credentials` requests to our IdP (Keycloak) still fail — but with a different, more specific error surfaced in the IdP's own audit log (not visible from litellm's side, only from the token endpoint's server-side logs): ``` error="invalid_request", reason="Invalid scopes: basic uma_protection Custom_Scope a2a-chat-ia-mcp-audience roles phone microprofile-jwt openid web-origins offline_access acr email service_account profile address", grant_type="client_credentials", client_auth_method="client-secret", username="service-account-<client>" ``` Client authentication itself **succeeds** here (Keycloak resolves the service-account user, confirming the secret is valid) — the request fails only because of the `scope` parameter litellm sends. The requested scope list is unusually large and includes scopes that are not, and could never sensibly be, assigned to this specific client (`microprofile-jwt`, `web-origins`, `acr`, several other realm-wide default/optional scopes). This looks like litellm is requesting the full `scopes_supported` list from the IdP's OIDC discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`) rather than a scope the operator configured (or no `scope` parameter at all, which is valid per RFC 6749 §4.4.2 and lets the IdP apply the client's default scopes). ### Expected behavior The `client_credentials` grant should either omit `scope` entirely (letting the IdP apply the client's configured default scopes, which is spec-compliant and what a plain `curl` grant with no `scope` param does successfully against the same client/IdP), or send only an operator-configured scope list — never every scope advertised by discovery metadata. ### Environment Same as Bug 1/2. ### Related issues Not yet searched for a matching open issue — flagging here since it was discovered as a direct consequence of investigating Bug 1. **Update: Bug 3 also breaks the interactive `authorization_code` flow, not just `client_credentials`** Confirmed this is not specific to `client_credentials`. Registering a second server with `oauth2_flow: authorization_code` (same `client_id`, plus an `issuer` so LiteLLM does RFC 8414 discovery instead of using manually-set `authorization_url`/`token_url`) and hitting LiteLLM's own `/{server_name}/authorize` endpoint produces a `307` redirect to the IdP's `/auth` endpoint whose `scope` query param is the **exact same** full discovery scope list: ``` Invalid scopes: basic uma_protection Custom_Scope a2a-chat-ia-mcp-audience roles phone microprofile-jwt openid web-origins offline_access acr email service_account profile address ``` i.e. once `issuer` is set for discovery, LiteLLM builds this over-broad `scope` value for **every** OAuth2 flow it drives (both the M2M token request and the interactive `/authorize` redirect), not just `client_credentials`. Same root cause, hits both the token-request call site and the `/authorize` redirect builder. This was confirmed via a real interactive login attempt — the actual Keycloak login page itself surfaces `Invalid scopes` (same string as the token-endpoint audit log entry seen with `client_credentials`), which rules out this being a `client_credentials`-only or backend-log-only artifact. Cópialo desde el primer ```markdown hasta el cierre y pégalo directo en el comentario de GitHub — al pegarlo ahí se va a renderizar bien.

signals.title: [Feature]: Support GPT-5.6 (Sol / Terra / Luna) via Amazon Bedrock Runtime
signals.text: ### Overview AWS [announced on 2026-08-17](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/08/amazon-bedrock-cross-region-openai-v2/) that the GPT-5.6 family — Sol, Terra, and Luna — is now available through the **Bedrock Runtime** data plane, distinct from the existing Bedrock Mantle path. LiteLLM currently only has entries for these models under `bedrock_mantle/openai.gpt-5.6-{sol,terra,luna}`. There is no equivalent under a `bedrock/` prefix to reach them via Runtime. ### Why this matters Bedrock Runtime introduces two routing modes not available through Mantle: - **Geo (US CRIS)** — routes within a predefined US geography - **Global** — routes across any commercial AWS Region where the model is available, at lower per-token cost and with the highest throughput during demand spikes This addresses a practical capacity limitation with the current Mantle setup: as of 2026-07 GPT-5.6 is only available in us-east-1 / us-east-2, whereas global inference via Runtime removes that constraint. ### Problem Attempting to call these models via the Runtime path today fails. There are no model cost/metadata entries for them under a `bedrock` (non-Mantle) provider, and manually registering a model using the `openai.gpt-5.6-*` IDs produces: ``` BedrockException - {"message":"{\"error\":{\"code\":\"unsupported_parameter\",\"message\":\"Unsupported parameter: 'max_tokens' is not supported with this model.\",\"param\":\"max_tokens\",\"type\":\"invalid_request_error\"}}"} ``` ### Expected behavior LiteLLM should support invoking `openai.gpt-5.6-sol`, `openai.gpt-5.6-terra`, and `openai.gpt-5.6-luna` via Amazon Bedrock Runtime, including support for the cross-region global inference endpoints, with correct parameter mapping for these models.

signals.title: [Bug]: `cache_control_injection_points` incorrectly invokes Dotprompt prompt management and requires `prompt_id`
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Requests to `/v1/chat/completions` return HTTP 500 when a cloud model is configured with: ```yaml cache_control_injection_points: - role: system location: message ``` This has been observed with `gemini-3.6-flash`, `claude-opus-4.8`, and other cloud models configured in a local LiteLLM deployment. The same model and request work when `cache_control_injection_points` is removed. When this parameter is enabled, LiteLLM unexpectedly calls the Dotprompt prompt-management integration while constructing the chat prompt. The request is an ordinary chat-completion request and does not reference a managed prompt, so it does not contain a `prompt_id`. `PromptManagementBase.get_chat_completion_prompt()` consequently raises: ```text ValueError: prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` LiteLLM wraps this local preprocessing exception as an `APIConnectionError`, retries it five times, attempts fallback handling, and ultimately returns HTTP 500. This appears to occur because cache-control injection is incorrectly activating, or being handled by, the Dotprompt prompt-management callback. Configuring cache-control injection should not cause an unrelated prompt-management integration to require `prompt_id`. ### Expected behavior LiteLLM should add the requested cache-control metadata to the matching system message and submit the completion to the provider without requiring prompt-management fields. If the selected provider or model does not support cache-control injection, LiteLLM should return an appropriate validation or unsupported-feature error. It should not invoke prompt management or require `prompt_id`. ### Actual behavior An ordinary completion enters the Dotprompt prompt-management path and fails before a provider response can be obtained because the request has no `prompt_id`. ### User Flow - Run a local LiteLLM Proxy deployment with a cloud-backed model such as `claude-opus-4.8` or `gemini-3.6-flash`. - Configure the model with `cache_control_injection_points` under `litellm_params`: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-4.8 litellm_params: model: <provider/model> api_key: os.environ/PROVIDER_API_KEY cache_control_injection_points: - role: system location: message ``` - Send a normal request containing a system message, without specifying `prompt_id` or any managed-prompt parameters: ```bash curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "claude-opus-4.8", "messages": [ { "role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant." }, { "role": "user", "content": "Hello" } ] }' ``` - Observe that the request returns HTTP 500 with: ```text prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` - Remove the following configuration: ```yaml cache_control_injection_points: - role: system location: message ``` - Restart or reload the proxy and repeat the same request. - Observe that the prompt-management error no longer occurs. ### Proof the bug occurs | Test Result | Outcome | | --- | --- | | Cloud model without `cache_control_injection_points` | Request proceeds without this error | | Same model and request with `cache_control_injection_points` | HTTP 500 | | Request without any managed-prompt fields | Dotprompt is still invoked | | Models observed | `gemini-3.6-flash`, `claude-opus-4.8`, and other configured cloud models | The stack trace proves that an ordinary completion unexpectedly enters Dotprompt prompt management: ```text litellm.main.completion -> litellm_logging_obj.get_chat_completion_prompt -> custom_logger.get_chat_completion_prompt -> dotprompt_manager.get_chat_completion_prompt -> PromptManagementBase.get_chat_completion_prompt -> ValueError: prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` Relevant trace excerpt: ```text File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/main.py", line 5076, in completion ) = litellm_logging_obj.get_chat_completion_prompt( File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py", line 701, in get_chat_completion_prompt ) = custom_logger.get_chat_completion_prompt( File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/integrations/dotprompt/dotprompt_manager.py", line 201, in get_chat_completion_prompt return PromptManagementBase.get_chat_completion_prompt( File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/integrations/prompt_management_base.py", line 168, in get_chat_completion_prompt raise ValueError("prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class") ValueError: prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` The error is then incorrectly surfaced as a provider connection failure: ```text 500 litellm.APIConnectionError: prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` LiteLLM retries the deterministic preprocessing failure: ```text LiteLLM Retried: 5 times, LiteLLM Max Retries: 5 ``` Fallback handling cannot recover from it: ```text No fallback model group found for original model_group=claude-opus-4.8 Error doing the fallback: litellm.APIConnectionError: prompt_id is required for Prompt Management Base class ``` This evidence shows that: 1. The exception originates in LiteLLM prompt preprocessing rather than in the cloud provider. 2. Dotprompt is invoked even though the request does not use a managed prompt. 3. Enabling `cache_control_injection_points` makes `prompt_id` incorrectly mandatory. 4. The issue is provider-independent because it occurs with multiple cloud models. 5. Retries and fallbacks cannot resolve the issue because every attempt encounters the same local preprocessing error. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.2 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: Background health checks load the entire (unbounded) LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable into every worker each cycle → excessive/near-OOM memory + DB storms at scale
signals.text: ## What happened? Two independent defects in the background health-check loop combine to storm the database every cycle (default 15 min) when running `use_shared_health_check: true` with multiple workers: **Bug 1 — DB persistence is not leader-gated:** `SharedHealthCheckManager` correctly gates the **probing** step (only the lock-holder sends health-check requests to LLM providers). But after probing, `_run_background_health_check()` unconditionally calls `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` on **every worker** (line ~3499 of `proxy_server.py`). Each worker runs `get_all_latest_health_checks()` — a `SELECT DISTINCT ON` full-table scan — plus per-model INSERTs. With N workers this multiplies DB load by N every cycle. **Bug 2 — HealthCheckTable is append-only with no retention:** `save_health_check_result()` in `PrismaClient` uses `.create()` (INSERT). There is no upsert and no pruning. The table grows unbounded. Because `get_all_latest_health_checks()` uses `DISTINCT ON (model_id, model_name)` ordered by `checked_at DESC`, Postgres must scan **all rows** to find the latest per model — there is no loose index-scan optimization for `DISTINCT ON`. **Combined impact at scale:** In our production environment (360 models, ~10 workers, 15-min cycle), the table grew to **3.9 million rows** in 64 days. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of `get_all_latest_health_checks()` shows: - **4.18 seconds** execution time - **~31 GB** buffer traffic (index + heap) - Scans all 3.9M rows to return 360 When ~10 workers run this simultaneously against a near-idle database (we use Aurora Serverless v2 with auto-scaling), it triggers a cold scale-up to max capacity, which causes connection churn, severs query-engine connections across all tasks, health saves fail, deployments get marked unavailable, and the proxy returns `No deployments available` 500s. We observed a **20.6% 5xx rate** during a 25-minute incident window. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure LiteLLM proxy with: ```yaml general_settings: use_shared_health_check: true background_health_checks: true health_check_interval: 900 # 15 min ``` 2. Deploy with multiple workers (e.g. 4+ Gunicorn workers or multiple pods behind a load balancer) and 100+ models in config. 3. Let the proxy run for several weeks. 4. Observe `LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable` row count growing linearly (models × cycles × workers per cycle): ```sql SELECT count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable"; -- After 64 days with 360 models, 10 workers: ~3.9M rows ``` 5. Observe that **every worker** calls `get_all_latest_health_checks()` each cycle, not just the leader: ```sql -- Proof of leaderless fan-out: distinct checked_by values within a single cycle SELECT checked_at, checked_by, count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable" WHERE checked_at > now() - interval '20 minutes' GROUP BY checked_at, checked_by ORDER BY checked_at DESC; -- Returns rows for EACH pod writing the same models <60s apart ``` 6. At sufficient table size, the `DISTINCT ON` read becomes multi-second, and concurrent execution from N workers causes DB saturation / connection exhaustion. ## Relevant log output ``` # EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the DISTINCT ON read (3.9M rows, 360 models): Unique (cost=0.56..2847163.44 rows=360 width=1389) (actual time=0.194..4183.021 rows=360 loops=1) -> Index Scan using ... on "LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable" (actual time=0.193..3922.574 rows=3900000 loops=1) Planning Time: 0.422 ms Execution Time: 4183.541 ms Buffers: shared hit=31457280 ``` ## Root Cause in Code **`proxy_server.py` ~L3498-3505** — `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` is called unconditionally regardless of whether this worker was the health-check leader: ```python # Save background health checks to database (non-blocking) _schedule_background_health_check_db_save( prisma_client, shared_health_manager, _llm_model_list, healthy_endpoints, unhealthy_endpoints, ) ``` **`utils.py` ~L5138** — `save_health_check_result()` uses `.create()` (INSERT), never upserts or prunes: ```python return await HealthCheckRepository(self).table.create(data=health_check_data) ``` **`utils.py` ~L5180-5187** — `get_all_latest_health_checks()` does `DISTINCT ON` over the full table: ```python return await HealthCheckRepository(self).table.find_many( distinct=["model_id", "model_name"], order=[ {"model_id": "asc"}, {"model_name": "asc"}, {"checked_at": "desc"}, ], ) ``` ## Suggested Fix **Short-term (two changes):** 1. **Leader-gate the DB persistence:** `SharedHealthCheckManager` already elects a leader for probing. Expose an `is_current_pod_leader` flag (set True when the pod acquires the lock or falls back to local probe; reset to False on cache hit). Gate `_schedule_background_health_check_db_save()` on it so exactly one pod does the read + write per cycle. When `shared_health_manager is None`, preserve the existing per-pod behavior. 2. **Add retention pruning:** After a successful save, the leader prunes rows older than a retention window (e.g. 7 days) via a batched, bounded DELETE. This caps the `DISTINCT ON` scan cost at O(recent rows) instead of O(all history). Batching (e.g. 10k rows per pass, max 50 passes) avoids long locks on the first run against a large backlog. **Long-term (architectural):** Replace the append-only `LiteLLM_HealthCheckTable` with a **one-row-per-model upsert** design (a `LiteLLM_HealthCheckLatest` table with `model_id` as primary key, upserted each cycle). This makes the "latest per model" read O(N models) — a simple `SELECT *` — instead of `DISTINCT ON` over unbounded history. History can be kept in the existing table with retention, or dropped entirely. ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ## What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.94.3
signals.author: Praveena-617

signals.title: [Bug]: azure/gpt-5.6* entries missing cache_creation_input_token_cost — cache writes billed at zero since v1.97.0
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Every `azure/gpt-5.6*` entry in the price map lacks `cache_creation_input_token_cost`, while its non-Azure counterpart has it. Since v1.97.0 correctly classifies Azure's `cache_write_tokens` as cache-creation tokens, those tokens now resolve to no rate and are billed at **zero**. This is a regression in effect, though not in code. Before v1.97.0 the same tokens were folded into plain input and under-reported by ~20%; now they are dropped entirely and under-report by ~98%. The fix for #33772 corrected the code path and the OpenAI entries, but the Azure entries were not updated to match. All eight Azure entries are missing the key; all four non-Azure counterparts have it: | Model | input_cost_per_token | cache_creation_input_token_cost | |---|---|---| | `gpt-5.6` | 5e-06 | 6.25e-06 | | `azure/gpt-5.6` | 5e-06 | **missing** | | `azure/us/gpt-5.6` | 5.5e-06 | **missing** | | `gpt-5.6-sol` | 5e-06 | 6.25e-06 | | `azure/gpt-5.6-sol` | 5e-06 | **missing** | | `azure/us/gpt-5.6-sol` | 5.5e-06 | **missing** | | `gpt-5.6-luna` | 2e-07 | 2.5e-07 | | `azure/gpt-5.6-luna` | 2e-07 | **missing** | | `azure/us/gpt-5.6-luna` | 2.2e-07 | **missing** | | `gpt-5.6-terra` | 2e-06 | 2.5e-06 | | `azure/gpt-5.6-terra` | 2e-06 | **missing** | | `azure/us/gpt-5.6-terra` | 2.2e-06 | **missing** | Azure prices cache writes at 1.25× input, same as OpenAI, so the values should mirror the non-Azure entries (with the 10% uplift already present on `azure/us/*`). **Expected:** a request whose prompt tokens are mostly cache writes is billed at the cache-creation rate. **Actual:** those tokens cost nothing, so spend is under-reported by ~98%. Not a duplicate of #36094 — that one is about the per-token input/output prices for Luna being wrong by 5×. This one is about a missing key across the whole gpt-5.6 Azure family causing cache-write tokens to price at zero. Fixing either leaves the other in place. ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a platform team charging back Azure OpenAI spend per team sees almost nothing billed for their RAG service, whose requests carry a large cached system prompt 1. Their RAG service sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with "model": "azure-gpt-5.6-sol" and a ~2,200-token system prompt 2. The response comes back 200 with "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 2219, "prompt_tokens_details": {"cache_write_tokens": 2217}} 3. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and the request shows $0.000225 spend 4. Their monthly Azure invoice for the same traffic is roughly 60× higher than the total the gateway reports, so per-team chargeback is unusable After a (hypothetical) fix: the same request is billed at the cache-write rate, and the gateway total lines up with the invoice 1. Their RAG service sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with "model": "azure-gpt-5.6-sol" and the same ~2,200-token system prompt 2. The response comes back 200 with the same usage object 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows that request at $0.014015 spend 4. The monthly total tracks the Azure invoice, so chargeback per team is accurate ### Proof the bug occurs **Config / setup the proxy ran with:** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: azure-gpt-5.6-sol litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5.6-sol api_base: os.environ/AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT api_version: "2025-04-01-preview" general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL ``` Live Azure OpenAI deployment, `gpt-5.6-sol`, GlobalStandard. Authentication is a workload identity, so no key appears in the config. **Version or commit:** v1.97.0 (the same request on v1.97.0 is compared against v1.94.2 below) **Commands and their full output:** Send a request whose prompt is large enough to trigger a cache write: ```bash python - <<'EOF' import json prefix = 'You are a documentation assistant. ' + ( 'The following is reference material about cloud architecture patterns. ' * 220) json.dump({"model": "azure-gpt-5.6-sol", "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": prefix}, {"role": "user", "content": "say ok"}], "max_tokens": 10}, open("req.json", "w")) EOF curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data @req.json | jq .usage ``` Output — the provider reports 2217 cache-write tokens: ```json { "completion_tokens": 5, "prompt_tokens": 2219, "total_tokens": 2224, "prompt_tokens_details": { "audio_tokens": 0, "cached_tokens": 0, "cache_write_tokens": 2217, "cache_creation_tokens": 2217 } } ``` What the gateway recorded for that request: ```bash curl -s "http://localhost:4000/spend/logs" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" | jq '.[-1] | {model, spend, prompt_tokens}' ``` ```json { "model": "azure/gpt-5.6-sol", "spend": 0.000225, "prompt_tokens": 2220 } ``` Correct value is `3 × 5e-6 + 2216 × 6.25e-6 + 5 × 3e-5 = 0.014015`, so this is 98% short. **Same request, three setups:** | Setup | recorded spend | vs correct | |---|---|---| | v1.94.2, price map | 0.011245 | −20% | | v1.97.0, price map | **0.000225** | **−98%** | | v1.97.0, prices declared in config | 0.001470 | correct | The third row is the workaround, and it confirms the price map entry is the only thing missing — nothing else changed: ```yaml - model_name: azure-gpt-5.6-sol litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5.6-sol input_cost_per_token: 0.000005 output_cost_per_token: 0.00003 cache_creation_input_token_cost: 0.00000625 cache_read_input_token_cost: 0.0000005 ``` (That run's request was mostly cache *reads* rather than writes, since the prefix was already cached: 2213 read + 8 write + 10 output = 2213×5e-7 + 8×6.25e-6 + 10×3e-5 = 0.0014565, matching the recorded 0.001470.) **Isolating it to the price map** — same code path, same usage object, the two entries differ only in whether the key exists: ```python import litellm from litellm.types.utils import Usage, PromptTokensDetailsWrapper details = PromptTokensDetailsWrapper(cached_tokens=0) details.cache_write_tokens = 2216 usage = Usage(prompt_tokens=2219, completion_tokens=5, total_tokens=2224, prompt_tokens_details=details) for model, provider in [("gpt-5.6-sol", "openai"), ("azure/gpt-5.6-sol", "azure")]: p, c = litellm.cost_calculator.generic_cost_per_token( model=model, usage=usage, custom_llm_provider=provider) print(f"{model}: {p + c:.8f}") ``` ``` gpt-5.6-sol: 0.01401500 azure/gpt-5.6-sol: 0.00016500 ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: `split_concatenated_json_objects` raises `JSONDecodeError` on a malformed remainder, aborting the whole multi-tool-call turn
signals.text: ### What happened? `split_concatenated_json_objects` (litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/common_utils.py) parses a raw string containing concatenated JSON objects (tool-call `arguments` from parallel tool calls). When one object in the sequence is truncated or otherwise malformed, `decoder.raw_decode(raw, idx)` raises `json.JSONDecodeError` uncaught, propagating out of the function and aborting the caller's (`parse_tool_call_arguments`) entire multi-tool-call turn — not just the one malformed call. ### Steps to Reproduce ```python from litellm.litellm_core_utils.prompt_templates.common_utils import ( split_concatenated_json_objects, ) split_concatenated_json_objects('{"a": 1}{"b": ') ``` Expected: returns `[{"a": 1}]` — the complete objects already decoded — so the caller can fall back to `{}` for the one unparseable tool call. Actual: raises `json.JSONDecodeError`. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Completions ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.94.3
signals.author: jimmychen-p72

signals.title: [Bug]: Perplexity Agent API models 400 on /v1/chat/completions unless the cost map happens to carry a reachable `mode: responses` entry
signals.text:
### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? Perplexity's Agent API namespaces its model ids with a `perplexity/` prefix, so a litellm deployment for one reads `model: perplexity/perplexity/<id>`, the routing prefix plus the model's own name. Those deployments answer on `/v1/responses` but return 400 on `/v1/chat/completions`, with Perplexity rejecting a name nobody wrote, e.g. `Invalid model 'perplexity/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b'` Whether an Agent API deployment works on chat completions comes down to whether the shipped cost map happens to carry a `mode: responses` entry that the model lookup actually reaches. `perplexity/perplexity/glm-5.2` has one, so it returns 200. Four models Perplexity serves today have no entry at all (`nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b`, `nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b`, `deepseek-v4-pro-0813`, `glm-5.3`), so they 400. `perplexity/perplexity/sonar` does have a `mode: responses` entry and still 400s, because the older `perplexity/sonar` chat entry wins the lookup and the request goes to Perplexity's chat endpoint instead of its Agent API `/v1/responses` needs none of that. It returns 200 for every one of these models, the four with no cost-map entry included, and the amount Perplexity metered comes back on the response I expected `/v1/chat/completions` to reach the same model `/v1/responses` reaches, since both point at one deployment. Related, on a different endpoint and with a different cause: #37716 ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer whose OpenAI-SDK app calls a Perplexity Agent API model gets a 400 naming a model they never asked for 1. Their proxy admin adds a deployment named `pplx-nemotron-ultra` pointing at `perplexity/perplexity/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` and restarts the proxy 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"model": "pplx-nemotron-ultra"` and get a 200 whose output text reads `pong` 3. They point their OpenAI SDK at the proxy and send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with the same `"model": "pplx-nemotron-ultra"` 4. They get a 400 reading `Invalid model 'perplexity/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b'. Permitted models can be found in the documentation at https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/getting-started/models.`, naming a model id neither they nor their admin ever wrote 5. Their admin swaps in `perplexity/perplexity/sonar`, the Agent API model litellm already ships pricing for, and the same POST to https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions returns 400 `Invalid model 'perplexity/sonar'` 6. Of the six Agent API deployments they try, only `perplexity/perplexity/glm-5.2` answers on https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions, so the endpoint looks healthy for one model and broken for every other one After a (hypothetical) fix: the same request answers on `/v1/chat/completions` exactly as it does on `/v1/responses` 1. Their proxy admin adds a deployment named `pplx-nemotron-ultra` pointing at `perplexity/perplexity/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` and restarts the proxy 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"model": "pplx-nemotron-ultra"` and get a 200 whose output text reads `pong` 3. They point their OpenAI SDK at the proxy and send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with the same `"model": "pplx-nemotron-ultra"` 4. They get a 200 whose message content reads `pong` 5. Their admin swaps in `perplexity/perplexity/sonar` and that deployment answers 200 on https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions too 6. All six Agent API deployments answer on https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions, and https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs records each call at the amount Perplexity metered ### Proof the bug occurs Config the proxy ran with (`pplx_missing.yaml`): ```yaml model_list: - model_name: pplx-glm-5.2 litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/glm-5.2 api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY - model_name: pplx-sonar litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/sonar api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY - model_name: pplx-nemotron-ultra litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY - model_name: pplx-nemotron-lightning litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY - model_name: pplx-deepseek-v4-pro litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/deepseek-v4-pro-0813 api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY - model_name: pplx-glm-5.3 litellm_params: model: perplexity/perplexity/glm-5.3 api_key: os.environ/PERPLEXITY_API_KEY general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 ``` Env vars: `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY=<redacted>`, and `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True` so the proxy reads the repo's own cost map rather than the one published from `main`, which does not carry the `perplexity/perplexity/*` entries yet. Nothing else was set Commit: `35416c702d84f10ef19335996d24de9657cc2038` on `litellm_internal_staging` (v1.99.0), started with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config pplx_missing.yaml --port 33958 --detailed_debug` Commands and their full output. signals.title: [Bug]: stream_chunk_builder raises IndexError/KeyError in build_base_response, truncating client SSE stream and skipping SpendLogs
signals.text: ### What happened? `ChunkProcessor.build_base_response()` reads the assistant role without guarding either the `choices` array bounds or the presence of a `role` key: ```python # litellm/litellm_core_utils/streaming_chunk_builder_utils.py first_chunk_with_choices: Final = next((c for c in chunks if c.get("choices")), chunk) role: Final = first_chunk_with_choices["choices"][0]["delta"]["role"] ``` Two distinct failures follow: 1. **`IndexError: list index out of range`** — when no chunk carries a non-empty `choices` array, `next()` returns its default (the *first* chunk), whose `choices` is `[]`. The `[0]` access then goes out of bounds. 2. **`KeyError: 'role'`** — when the first choice's `delta` omits `role` or is `{}`. Either one propagates out of `stream_chunk_builder()` as: ``` litellm.APIError: Error building chunks for logging/streaming usage calculation ``` `proxy_server.async_data_generator()` catches it and writes it into the response stream: ```python error_returned = json.dumps({"error": proxy_exception.to_dict()}) yield f"data: {error_returned}\n\n" ``` Control then goes straight to `finally`, so **`data: [DONE]` is never emitted**. Note the loop directly below the offending line already guards correctly with `len(chunk["choices"]) > 0`, so this looks like a simple omission rather than intent. ### Impact This is not only a logging-path bug. Two user-visible consequences: - **The client's stream is truncated.** The user has already received part of the answer, then the stream stops and an error frame arrives with no `[DONE]`. HTTP status is still 200, because SSE headers are flushed before the failure — so this does not show up as a 5xx in proxy access logs. - **The request is missing from SpendLogs**, so it is never billed. In our production proxy this hit Anthropic/Claude streaming intermittently — a handful of requests per day across a week. Successful responses in the same second were 19KB–339KB; the failing ones returned only ~360 bytes (just the error frame) after 8–38s. ### Relevant log output ```shell LiteLLM:ERROR: main.py:7815 - litellm.main.py::stream_chunk_builder() - Exception occurred - list index out of range Traceback (most recent call last): File "litellm/litellm_core_utils/streaming_handler.py", line 2147, in __anext__ raise StopAsyncIteration StopAsyncIteration During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred: Traceback (most recent call last): File "litellm/main.py", line 7561, in stream_chunk_builder response = processor.build_base_response(chunks) File "litellm/litellm_core_utils/streaming_chunk_builder_utils.py", line 123, in build_base_response role = first_chunk_with_choices["choices"][0]["delta"]["role"] ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^ IndexError: list index out of range LiteLLM Proxy:ERROR: proxy_server.py:7081 - litellm.proxy.proxy_server.async_data_generator(): Exception occured - litellm.APIError: Error building chunks for logging/streaming usage calculation ``` ### Reproduction ```python from litellm.litellm_core_utils.streaming_chunk_builder_utils import ChunkProcessor def mk(choices, **kw): d = {"id": "c1", "object": "chat.completion.chunk", "created": 1, "model": "claude-opus-4-8", "choices": choices} d.update(kw) return d cases = { "all-empty-choices": [mk([]), mk([])], "usage-only frames": [mk([], usage={"prompt_tokens": 10}), mk([], usage={"completion_tokens": 0})], "delta without role": [mk([{"index": 0, "delta": {"content": "Hi"}, "finish_reason": None}])], "delta empty dict": [mk([{"index": 0, "delta": {}, "finish_reason": None}])], } for name, chunks in cases.items(): try: ChunkProcessor(chunks=list(chunks)).build_base_response(list(chunks)) print(f"[ok] {name}") except Exception as e: print(f"[fail] {name} -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}") ``` Output on v1.88.1 and on current `litellm_internal_staging`: ``` [fail] all-empty-choices -> IndexError: list index out of range [fail] usage-only frames -> IndexError: list index out of range [fail] delta without role -> KeyError: 'role' [fail] delta empty dict -> KeyError: 'role' ``` ### Relation to existing issues #32051 and #32951 report `KeyError('choices')` — a *missing* `choices` key. #34382 and #32203 address that by switching to `c.get("choices")`. Those changes do not fix this report: here `choices` is **present but empty**, so `.get("choices")` returns `[]` (falsy), `next()` skips it, and the default fallback lands on a chunk that still indexes out of range. Neither PR touches the `["choices"][0]` access itself. ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.88.1, and the same code is present unchanged on `litellm_internal_staging` as of 2026-08-21 (latest release v1.97.0). ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signals.title: [Bug]: /v1/responses silently fake-streams Azure deployments with custom names, base_model is ignored by the streaming capability check
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? We route an Azure OpenAI provisioned (PTU) deployment through the LiteLLM proxy. Like most PTU deployments it has a custom deployment name (`gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu`), so the model entry declares `base_model` for cost tracking, the setup recommended in https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/custom_pricing `stream: true` requests to `/v1/responses` for this model return an SSE response, but no event arrives until the entire completion is finished: every event is delivered in a single burst at the end, and the deltas are synthetic 5-character chunks. Azure's diagnostic logs show the underlying call as a non-streaming request, so LiteLLM silently dropped `stream=true` and synthesized the events afterwards. Time-to-first-token equals total latency, which caused a production latency incident for us on 2026-08-18 Expected: `stream=true` is forwarded to Azure. LiteLLM cannot know the capabilities of an arbitrary deployment name, but the entry's `base_model`, which LiteLLM already trusts for cost calculation, identifies the underlying model, and that model streams Why it happens, verified against v1.92.0 and current litellm_internal_staging: the Responses API decides native vs fake streaming by looking up only the routed model name in the model cost map (`supports_native_streaming`), and converts "model not found" into "does not support streaming"; `model_info.base_model` is never consulted. The router registration that could bridge the gap writes deployment metadata under a double-prefixed key (`azure/azure/gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu`) whenever `litellm_params.custom_llm_provider` is set explicitly, so the capability lookup can never hit it Reproduction condition: `litellm_params.custom_llm_provider` set explicitly, which is the shape DB-managed deployments typically have (our rows are created via /model/new with it set). Omitting it happens to register a usable cost-map key for the deployment name, which masks the bug in minimal configs. `api_version` does not matter, reproduced identically on `2025-04-01-preview` and `v1` On duplicates: the same defect was reported as #21090 (identical call chain, vLLM-served custom models, tool events silently dropped) and auto-closed as stale without a fix. This report adds the Azure `base_model` angle, the router-registration root cause, the exact reproduction condition and measured evidence. The wider pattern of capability gates resolving against the deployment name while only cost tracking consults `base_model` also produced #31243 (reasoning_effort gate, closed but its fix PR unmerged per the comments), #12744 (o3 vs dumbo_o3, streaming differed with Base Model set, stale-closed while reproducible), #27717 and #28782 ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer streaming from a PTU-backed model gets no first-token latency benefit 1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `{"model": "gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu", "stream": true, "input": "..."}` 2. The connection stays silent for the entire generation, then all SSE events arrive at once: for a 60 second answer that is 60 seconds with no output 3. They check the provider side and the Azure diagnostic logs show the request as a non-streaming call even though they asked for a stream After a (hypothetical) fix: the same request streams for real 1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `{"model": "gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu", "stream": true, "input": "..."}` 2. Delta events start arriving within the model's normal first-token latency and continue progressively 3. The Azure diagnostic logs show the request as a streaming call ### Proof the bug occurs Config the proxy ran with (the Azure resource holds a deployment named `gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu` backed by the `gpt-5.4` model; env vars are the standard Azure service principal set, values redacted as secrets): ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu litellm_params: model: azure/gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu custom_llm_provider: azure api_base: os.environ/AZURE_API_BASE api_version: "2025-04-01-preview" tenant_id: os.environ/AZURE_TENANT_ID client_id: os.environ/AZURE_CLIENT_ID client_secret: os.environ/AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET model_info: base_model: azure/gpt-5.4 general_settings: master_key: sk-proof-1234 ``` Version or commit: litellm_internal_staging `ff02d5cfc0` Commands and their output: ```bash litellm --config proof.yaml --port 41234 ``` ```bash START=$EPOCHREALTIME curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:41234/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-proof-1234" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"gpt-5.4-csvo-ptu","input":"Write a numbered list counting from 1 to 150, one number per line. No other text.","stream":true}' | while IFS= read -r line; do [ -n "$line" ] && echo "$EPOCHREALTIME ${line:0:60}"; done > run.log awk -v t0="$START" '/output_text.delta/{n++; if(!d){d=1; fd=$1-t0}} {last=$1-t0} END{printf "events %d | text deltas %d | first delta at %.2fs | last event at %.2fs\n", NR, n, fd, last}' run.log ``` ``` events 108 | text deltas 99 | first delta at 3.47s | last event at 3.48s ``` run.log, first two lines, first delta and last line: the whole stream lands in one 10ms window after the full generation ``` 1787300206.421098 data: {"type":"response.created","response":{"id":"resp_7cVH 1787300206.421935 data: {"type":"response.in_progress","response":{"id":"resp_ 1787300206.422492 data: {"type":"response.output_text.delta","item_id":"msg_08 1787300206.429131 data: [DONE] ``` For comparison, the same commit plus a patch that lets the capability lookup fall back to `base_model` gives, for the same request: `events 308 | text deltas 299 | first delta at 2.21s | last event at 7.57s`, native token deltas arriving progressively ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? reproduced on v1.92.0 and current litellm_internal_staging (ff02d5cfc0, 2026-08-21)

signals.title: [Bug]: RetryPolicy.InternalServerErrorRetries is silently ignored in get_num_retries_from_retry_policy
signals.text: ## Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ## What happened? `RetryPolicy` defines `InternalServerErrorRetries` as a field in `litellm/types/router.py`, but `get_num_retries_from_retry_policy()` in `litellm/router_utils/get_retry_from_policy.py` has no branch for `InternalServerError`. The function handles five error types (`AuthenticationError`, `Timeout`, `RateLimitError`, `ContentPolicyViolationError`, `BadRequestError`) and omits `InternalServerError`. The value is accepted in config, validates against the pydantic model, and is never read at runtime. This is the retry-side twin of #29283, which reports the identical omission for `AllowedFailsPolicy.InternalServerErrorAllowedFails` in `get_allowed_fails_from_policy()`. That issue has been open since 2026-05-29. Both policy resolvers are missing the same error type, in two different functions, so a fix for one will not fix the other. Impact: upstream 5xx is the most common transient failure worth retrying, and it is the one error class the retry policy cannot express. Because `router.py` only overrides `num_retries` when the resolver returns non-`None`: ```python if _retry_policy_retries is not None: num_retries = _retry_policy_retries _retry_policy_applies = True ``` a configured `InternalServerErrorRetries` falls through to the global `num_retries`. Worse, `_retry_policy_applies` stays `False`, so the request additionally goes through `should_retry_this_error()`, which a caller who set an explicit per-error policy is not expecting to apply. The silent-acceptance part is what makes this costly: an operator who configures `InternalServerErrorRetries: 3` and nothing else gets zero 5xx retries, with no warning at startup and no error at request time. ## User Flow Configure a per-error retry policy on the proxy, scoped to a model group: ```yaml router_settings: model_group_retry_policy: my-model: TimeoutErrorRetries: 3 InternalServerErrorRetries: 3 RateLimitErrorRetries: 2 ``` Expected: an upstream 500 is retried 3 times. Actual: `InternalServerErrorRetries` is never read. The resolver returns `None` for `InternalServerError`, so the router falls back to the global `num_retries` (0 by default), and a 500 is not retried at all. ## Proof the bug occurs Resolving each error class through the public accessor. Timeout and RateLimit come back from the policy; InternalServerError does not: ```python import litellm from litellm import Router pol = {"TimeoutErrorRetries": 3, "InternalServerErrorRetries": 3, "RateLimitErrorRetries": 2, "BadRequestErrorRetries": 0, "AuthenticationErrorRetries": 0, "ContentPolicyViolationErrorRetries": 0} rt = Router(model_list=[{"model_name": "m", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-4o-mini"}}], model_group_retry_policy={"m": pol}) for exc, label in ((litellm.Timeout("t", "openai", "m"), "Timeout"), (litellm.InternalServerError("e", "m", "openai"), "InternalServerError"), (litellm.RateLimitError("r", "m", "openai"), "RateLimit"), (litellm.BadRequestError("b", "m", "openai"), "BadRequest")): print(label, rt.get_num_retries_from_retry_policy(exception=exc, model_group="m")) ``` Output: ``` Timeout 3 InternalServerError None RateLimit 2 BadRequest 0 ``` The field validates fine, which is why this is easy to miss: ```python >>> from litellm.types.router import RetryPolicy >>> RetryPolicy(**pol).model_dump() {'BadRequestErrorRetries': 0, 'AuthenticationErrorRetries': 0, 'TimeoutErrorRetries': 3, 'RateLimitErrorRetries': 2, 'ContentPolicyViolationErrorRetries': 0, 'InternalServerErrorRetries': 3} ``` Suggested fix, matching the shape of the existing branches in `get_retry_from_policy.py`: ```python if ( isinstance(exception, InternalServerError) and retry_policy.InternalServerErrorRetries is not None ): return retry_policy.InternalServerErrorRetries ``` Two notes on ordering, since `litellm.InternalServerError` and the other mapped exceptions can overlap depending on how a provider maps status codes: the new branch should sit alongside the others rather than ahead of `Timeout`, and it is worth confirming no provider maps a 500 onto `BadRequestError`, which would shadow it. ## What part of LiteLLM is this about? Router / Proxy (retry and fallback logic) ## What LiteLLM version are you on ? 1.97.0 ## Twitter / LinkedIn details n/a --- AI assistance used: Yes Claude Code was used to trace the code path and draft this report; the reproduction above was run against a live 1.97.0 deployment.

signals.title: [Bug]: keys with key_type="llm_api" get 403 on /model/info, /v1/model/info, /v2/model/info and /model_group/info
signals.text: ### What happened A key created with `key_type="llm_api"` can call models but cannot read model metadata. `handle_key_type` sets `allowed_routes=["llm_api_routes"]` (`litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/key_management_endpoints.py:476-477`), and `LiteLLMRoutes.llm_api_routes` (`litellm/proxy/_types.py:518-528`) covers `/models` and `/v1/models` but none of the model-metadata endpoints, which live in `info_routes` (`litellm/proxy/_types.py:529-551`): `/model/info`, `/v1/model/info`, `/v2/model/info`, `/model_group/info` `RouteChecks.is_virtual_key_allowed_to_call_route` therefore returns 403 for all four, so an OpenAI-compatible client that discovers pricing, mode or context-window limits from `/model_group/info` gets nothing while `/v1/chat/completions` on the very same key works. The check runs in `should_call_route` before any role branching (`litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py:2536`), so this applies to every caller holding such a key, including one whose user row is `proxy_admin` This looks like a gap rather than a deliberate restriction: the same key group already reaches `/v1/models`, and `llm_api_routes` already carries a method-aware carve-out for the read-only MCP server discovery endpoints (`litellm/proxy/auth/route_checks.py:155-166`), which is the same shape of problem ### Reproduction Proxy on `localhost:4000` with a Postgres backend, one deployment in `config.yaml`, `master_key: sk-e2e-1234` ```bash # 1. create a key with the llm_api preset KEY=$(curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4000/key/generate \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-e2e-1234" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"key_type":"llm_api","key_alias":"repro"}' | jq -r .key) # 2. confirm the preset that /key/generate applied curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4000/key/info?key=$KEY" -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-e2e-1234" \ | jq '{key_type: .info.key_type, allowed_routes: .info.allowed_routes}' # 3. metadata endpoints vs /v1/models with the same key for r in /v1/model/info /model/info /v2/model/info /model_group/info /v1/models; do printf '%-20s %s\n' "$r" "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4000$r")" done ``` Output: ``` {"key_type":"llm_api","allowed_routes":["llm_api_routes"]} /v1/model/info 403 /model/info 403 /v2/model/info 403 /model_group/info 403 /v1/models 200 ``` Response body on any of the four: ```json {"detail":"Virtual key is not allowed to call this route. Only allowed to call routes: ['llm_api_routes']. Tried to call route: /model_group/info"} ``` ### Expected behavior A key scoped to `llm_api_routes` should be able to read metadata for the models it is already allowed to call, the same way it can list them through `/v1/models` ### Suggested fix A GET-only carve-out inside the virtual-key check, mirroring `_is_get_mcp_server_discovery_route`, keeps the blast radius at the ACL layer: ```python _MODEL_DISCOVERY_ROUTES = frozenset( ("/model/info", "/v1/model/info", "/v2/model/info", "/model_group/info") ) @staticmethod def _is_get_model_discovery_route(route: str, request: Optional[Request]) -> bool: if request is None or request.method.upper() != "GET": return False return route in _MODEL_DISCOVERY_ROUTES ``` called next to the existing MCP carve-out under `if allowed_route == "llm_api_routes":` Worth noting why simply appending the four paths to `LiteLLMRoutes.llm_api_routes` is a heavier change: `RouteChecks.is_llm_api_route` membership also drives budget reservation (`litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/budget_reservation.py:141`), cost tracking (`litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py:74`), tag routing and the global-spend gate (`litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py:341,359`), plus `_check_llm_api_route_access` (`litellm/proxy/auth/route_checks.py:779`), none of which should treat a metadata GET as an LLM call. Both `/models` and `/v1/models` already need explicit exclusions in two of those call sites for the same reason The writes on the shared prefix (`/model/new`, `/model/update`, `/model/delete`) are separate paths, so neither variant reaches them, and both `/model/info` and `/model_group/info` already scope their response to the caller's model access One thing worth a maintainer's call: `remove_sensitive_info_from_deployment` (`litellm/proxy/common_utils/openai_endpoint_utils.py:29-47`) strips `api_key`, `client_secret`, `vertex_credentials` and the AWS keys, but leaves `api_base` in the `/model/info` response. If that is considered infrastructure detail an LLM-API key should not see, the carve-out could cover `/model_group/info` only, whose response carries no `api_base` ### Related observability gap `should_call_route` is called outside the `try/except` that routes authorization failures through `UserAPIKeyAuthExceptionHandler._handle_authentication_error` (`litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py:2536` vs `2543-2559`), so a route denial raises straight to FastAPI and never gets the log line that budget or model-access denials get. In practice a 403 from this path leaves nothing in the proxy log beyond the uvicorn access line, which makes it hard to tell which key was denied. Happy to file that separately if it is worth its own issue ### Relevant log output ``` INFO: 10.245.4.246:33766 - "GET /v2/model/info HTTP/1.1" 403 Forbidden ``` ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.94.2

signals.title: [Bug]: azure/us/ and azure/eu/ gpt-4o-2024-11-20 missing cache_read_input_token_cost  at present cache reads billed at zero
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 and azure/eu/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 are missing cache_read_input_token_cost in the price map. All other gpt-4o data-zone entries (e.g., azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-08-06, azure/eu/gpt-4o-2024-08-06) carry the field at 1.375e-06 (1.1x the OpenAI rate of 1.25e-06). The 2024-11-20 variants were never updated to match, so any cache-read tokens on those deployments resolve to no rate and are billed at $0 by LiteLLM. ### User Flow Before a fix: a team using azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 with a large cached system prompt sees cache reads billed at zero 1. They POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with model "azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-11-20" and a prompt containing a large previously-cached block 2. Azure returns usage with prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens populated (e.g., 5000 cached tokens) 3. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and see the request logged at a spend that reflects only non-cached tokens: cache-read tokens contribute $0 instead of the correct ~$0.007 for 5000 tokens After a fix: the same request is billed correctly 1-2. Same steps 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows the request at full spend including cache-read tokens at 1.375e-06 per token ### Proof the bug occurs Verified on commit ff02d5cfc0 (litellm_internal_staging, 2026-08-21). Direct inspection of model_prices_and_context_window.json: model input_cost_per_token cache_read_input_token_cost ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ gpt-4o-2024-11-20 2.5e-06 1.25e-06 azure/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 2.75e-06 1.25e-06 azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 2.75e-06 None ← bug azure/eu/gpt-4o-2024-11-20 2.75e-06 None ← bug azure/us/gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (control) 2.75e-06 1.375e-06 ← working Every other azure/us/ and azure/eu/ gpt-4o entry applies the standard 1.1x data-zone uplift to cache_read_input_token_cost. These two entries were simply never populated. No proxy or provider API call needed to reproduce: the field is missing from the static pricing config. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? SDK (litellm Python package) ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details https://www.linkedin.com/in/abhay-tiwari-/

signals.title: [Feature]  Semantic Agent Discovery — Search API + MCP Tool
signals.text: ## Summary Add semantic/hybrid search capability to the A2A agent registry with two access patterns: 1. **REST API** — search endpoint for UI, scripts, and direct API consumers 2. **MCP tool** — so any MCP-connected agent or app can discover agents as part of its tool chain ## Problem Current agent discovery is limited to: - `GET /v1/agents` — returns full list, requires manual scanning - `GET /a2a/{agent_id}/.well-known/agent-card.json` — requires knowing the exact agent ID As the number of registered agents grows, finding the right agent becomes increasingly difficult. There is no way to search by capability, skill description, or intent. For agentic workflows this is a bigger gap — an orchestrator agent has no programmatic way to ask "which agent can help with X?" before routing a task. --- ## Proposed Solution ### 1. REST Endpoint Hybrid search (semantic + keyword) over agent metadata — names, descriptions, skills, tags, input/output modes. > *Sample endpoint and response below — schema is illustrative and can be extended based on implementation needs.* ``` GET /v1/agents/search?q=translate+a+PDF+document&limit=5 ``` ```json { "results": [ { "agent_id": "abc-123", "agent_name": "clinical-summarizer", "description": "Summarizes clinical trial protocols and results", "score": 0.92, "matching_skills": ["protocol-summary", "results-extraction"] } ] } ``` ### 2. MCP Tool — `search_agents` Expose the same search as an MCP tool so any MCP-connected agent or application can discover agents programmatically. > *Sample tool definition below — schema is illustrative and can be extended based on implementation needs.* ```json { "name": "search_agents", "description": "Search registered A2A agents by natural language query.", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": { "type": "string", "description": "Natural language search query" }, "limit": { "type": "integer", "default": 5 } }, "required": ["query"] } } ``` This enables patterns like: - An orchestrator uses `search_agents` as a planning step before delegating sub-tasks - The UI calls the MCP tool for its search bar - A coding assistant finds a "code review" agent, then calls it via A2A --- ## Reference Implementation AWS Bedrock AgentCore Agent Registry provides search and MCP access: - **Hybrid search** (semantic + keyword): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry-key-capabilities.html#registry-hybrid-search - **Search API**: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry-searching.html - **MCP endpoint**: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry-key-capabilities.html#registry-mcp-endpoint --- ## Scope - Hybrid search backend (semantic + keyword) over agent card fields - ACL-aware — search results filtered by caller's agent permissions - Results ranked by relevance score - Two access patterns (REST + MCP) sharing the same search backend ## Impact - Improves agent discoverability as the registry scales - Enables agentic orchestration patterns (agents finding other agents) - Aligns with AWS Agent Registry search + MCP capabilities

signals.title: SendGrid: support inline CID logo attachment to avoid external content warnings
signals.text: ## Problem Email clients (especially Microsoft Outlook) block external images in emails sent via SendGrid, prompting recipients with a **"Do you want to download external content?"** warning before rendering the logo. This happens because `SendGridEmailLogger.send_email()` sends HTML with an external `` URL. When the email was sent via SMTP through a corporate mail relay, Outlook trusted the sender and loaded images automatically. With SendGrid, the email originates from an external sender, so Outlook treats all linked content as untrusted. ## Proposed Solution Support embedding the logo as an **inline CID attachment** in the SendGrid Mail Send API payload. When a logo file path is configured, the image should be base64-encoded and attached with `disposition: inline` and a `content_id`, then the `{email_logo_url}` reference in the HTML body should be replaced with `cid:`. ## Suggested Changes ### 1. `litellm_enterprise/enterprise_callbacks/send_emails/sendgrid_email.py` **In `__init__`:** - Read a new env var `EMAIL_LOGO_PATH` (file path to the logo image) - If set, read the file, base64-encode it, and store as a pre-built attachment dict: ```python { "content": "", "type": "image/png", "filename": "logo.png", "disposition": "inline", "content_id": "logo" } ``` - If the file is missing or unset, fall back to the current external URL behavior (no breaking change) **In `send_email()`:** - If the logo attachment is available: 1. Replace the `EMAIL_LOGO_URL` value in `html_body` with `cid:logo` 2. Add `"attachments": []` to the SendGrid JSON payload ### 2. No template changes needed The existing `{email_logo_url}` placeholder in email templates (`key_created_email.py`, `key_rotated_email.py`, `user_invitation_email.py`) stays as-is. The URL-to-CID replacement happens at send time in `send_email()`. ### 3. No changes to `base_email.py` The `EmailParams.logo_url` resolution logic remains unchanged. The CID substitution is isolated to the SendGrid transport layer. ## Why This Matters - **Outlook desktop** (the most common corporate email client) blocks external images by default for emails from external senders - **CID inline attachments** are rendered without warnings in all major email clients (Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail, Thunderbird) - The logo file is only ~5 KB, so the email size increase is negligible - SMTP-based sending did not have this issue because corporate mail relays are trusted senders ## Environment - litellm version: 1.94.3 - Email provider: SendGrid (Mail Send API v3) - Affected email client: Microsoft Outlook (desktop and OWA) ## Workaround We are currently patching `sendgrid_email.py` at container startup to add this behavior. Would be great to have native support so we can drop the patch.

signals.title: [Bug]: Gemini thought signature is embedded in the tool call id, so any client that normalizes ids breaks the next turn
signals.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ### Not a duplicate of #25322 GitHub flagged #25322 as a possible duplicate. It is the **opposite** failure in the same area, and the two fixes do not overlap: | | #25322 | This issue | |---|---|---| | Endpoint | `/v1/messages` (Anthropic format, Claude Code) | `/v1/responses` and `/v1/chat/completions` | | What goes wrong | The signature is **never captured**, because Gemini put it on a separate thought part | The signature **is** captured and **is** sent back, but corrupted in transit | | What Google says | `Function call is missing a thought_signature in functionCall parts` | `Base64 decoding failed for "AY89a1/_57b05e78dc"` | | Symptom | The model degenerates: garbage replies, repetition loops | Hard `400`, the session cannot continue | Worth noting the two interact: #25322 treats embedding the signature in `tool_call_id` as the correct mechanism and asks for it to be fed in more cases. **Fixing #25322 alone would make this issue fire more often, not less**, because more tool calls would end up carrying a multi-KB id that clients then normalize. --- For Gemini models the proxy returns Google's `thoughtSignature` in two places: * `tool_calls[].provider_specific_fields.thought_signature` * appended to `tool_calls[].id` after a `__thought__` separator Neither is a key a generic OpenAI-compatible client knows about, and the second one is actively harmful: `id` is by convention a short identifier, so clients normalize it. Measured against Vertex Gemini 3, the returned tool call id ranges from **843 to 4423 characters** depending on the call. On `/v1/responses` the same blob is placed in **both `id` and `call_id`**. When a client normalizes that id, the embedded signature is mangled. On the next turn the proxy finds the `__thought__` separator, takes everything after it, and forwards it to Vertex as `thoughtSignature` without validating it. Google rejects the request: Invalid value at 'contents[1].parts[0].thought_signature' (TYPE_BYTES), Base64 decoding failed for "AY89a1/_57b05e78dc" The same corruption produces a second, different error text when the mangled value happens to still be valid base64, which makes this easy to miss when grepping logs: "message": "Invalid thought signature.", "status": "INVALID_ARGUMENT" There is no way to opt out: checked v1.83.14-stable, v1.90.0, v1.96.0 and main, the embedding is an unconditional `if thought_signature:`. ### Suggested fix **1. Also emit the signature at `tool_calls[].thought_signature` (top level).** Additive, breaks nothing. It matters because clients already read that key: OpenClaw captures `tool_calls[].thought_signature` generically for any OpenAI-compatible provider, support that was added for Venice, which returns the signature at exactly that key (OpenClaw #119591 / #119783). **2. Read the same key on the way in.** Today the lookup checks `provider_specific_fields`, the function's `provider_specific_fields`, and the id, but not the top level. Emitting without reading would only work in one direction. **3. Independently, validate before injecting.** If the extracted value does not base64-decode, fall back to the dummy skip-validator signature instead of forwarding it. That alone turns a hard 400 into a graceful degradation, and it is a much smaller change than 1 and 2. Item 3 is worth doing on its own: any client that normalizes the id today produces a user-visible error that the proxy could absorb. ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix — the agent answers the first question, then every following turn fails and the conversation is dead.** 1. An operator asks a Telegram assistant (built on OpenClaw) a question that requires a tool. 2. The client sends `POST https://<proxy>/v1/responses` with `model: gemini-3.1-pro-preview` and one function tool. 3. `200` comes back with a `function_call` item whose `call_id` is 1223 characters long: `call_2156408__thought__AY89a1/Iab3+RVjKCabD+h7qYLWIf2BWZ9CZDSDoMZpQytG...` 4. The client stores that `call_id`. Because it is an identifier, it normalizes it into something id-shaped, ending up with a 41 character value such as `AY89a1_S3YvIpUCcBTFSgDfesRLDnA_775ff49bcd`. 5. The client runs the tool and sends the next turn, echoing back the normalized `call_id` together with the `function_call_output`. 6. The proxy answers `400`: `Invalid value at 'contents[1].parts[0].thought_signature' (TYPE_BYTES), Base64 decoding failed for "AY89a1/_57b05e78dc"`. 7. The operator sees `LLM request failed` in the chat. Retrying does not help: the broken value is now part of the conversation history, so every following turn fails the same way and the session cannot progress. **After a (hypothetical) fix — the same conversation continues normally.** 1. An operator asks the same Telegram assistant the same question that requires a tool. 2. The client sends the same `POST https://<proxy>/v1/responses` with `model: gemini-3.1-pro-preview` and one function tool. 3. `200` comes back with a `function_call` item whose `call_id` is short, such as `call_2156408`, and the signature arrives in its own field on the tool call instead of inside the id. 4. The client stores both. The `call_id` is already id-shaped, so normalizing it changes nothing, and the signature is kept separately and untouched. 5. The client runs the tool and sends the next turn, echoing back the short `call_id`, the `function_call_output`, and the signature exactly as received. 6. The proxy answers `200` and the model produces the final message. 7. The operator gets the answer and can keep asking follow-up questions in the same conversation. ### Proof the bug occurs Captured against a self-hosted LiteLLM proxy on Kubernetes, hitting real Vertex AI. Host and keys redacted, everything else verbatim. **Config / setup the proxy ran with:** model_list: - model_name: gemini-3.1-pro-preview litellm_params: model: vertex_ai/gemini-3.1-pro-preview vertex_project: <redacted> vertex_location: global vertex_credentials: <service account JSON, redacted> **Version or commit:** v1.90.0. The same code path is present in v1.83.14-stable, v1.96.0 and main. **Commands and their full output:** #### 1. `/v1/responses`, first turn: the returned `call_id` carries the signature curl -s -X POST "$PROXY/v1/responses" -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @turn1.json turn1.json: {"model":"gemini-3.1-pro-preview", "input":"What is the weather in Santiago? Use the tool.", "tools":[{"type":"function","name":"get_weather", "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}}], "tool_choice":"required"} Output, trimmed to the relevant item: {"status":"completed", "output":[{"type":"function_call", "id":"call_2156408__thought__AY89a1/Iab3+RVjKCabD+h7qYLWIf2BWZ9CZDSDoMZpQytG...", "call_id":"call_2156408__thought__AY89a1/Iab3+RVjKCabD+h7qYLWIf2BWZ9CZDSDoMZpQytG...", "name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\": \"Santiago\"}"}]} `id` and `call_id` are both 1223 characters. #### 2. `/v1/responses`, second turn, `call_id` echoed verbatim: works Same request with `input` containing the `function_call` and a `function_call_output`, both using the 1223 character `call_id` unchanged. HTTP 200 — "The weather in Santiago is 21 C." #### 3. `/v1/responses`, second turn, `call_id` normalized: fails Identical to 2 with the `call_id` shortened the way an identifier normalizer would (`sanitized[:30] + "_" + sha256hex[:10]`), giving `call_2156408__thought__AY89a1/_57b05e78dc`: HTTP 400 litellm.BadRequestError: Vertex_aiException BadRequestError - { "error": { "code": 400, "message": "Invalid value at 'contents[1].parts[0].thought_signature' (TYPE_BYTES), Base64 decoding failed for \"AY89a1/_57b05e78dc\"", "status": "INVALID_ARGUMENT", "details": [{"@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.rpc.BadRequest", "fieldViolations": [{"field": "contents[1].parts[0].thought_signature"}]}] } } #### 4. `/v1/chat/completions`: same bug, cause is endpoint independent First turn returns `tool_calls[0].id` of 859 characters (`call_2254344__thought__AY89a19rfaQstNXhYomMSsTSpNLVRjsNCuBX+b2ZYUcVnGF...`) plus `provider_specific_fields.thought_signature` of 836 characters. Replaying the history with the id normalized to `call_2158562__thought__AY89a1/_ee781c9832`: HTTP 400 litellm.BadRequestError: Vertex_aiException BadRequestError - { "error": {"code": 400, "message": "Invalid value at 'contents[1].parts[0].thought_signature' (TYPE_BYTES), Base64 decoding failed for \"AY89a1/_ee781c9832\""} } #### Scale, from the same proxy One client, 19 failed requests over a month on this exact error, up to 22% of that client's calls in the worst hour, because once a corrupted signature enters the history every later turn fails. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.90.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details https://www.linkedin.com/in/joaquint/
