signals.title: fix(proxy): group Codex turns under one session id
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Every Codex turn logs as its own session, never grouped - Codex sends `session-id` unprefixed, so LiteLLM ignores it - `is_codex_user_agent` also missed the real `codex-tui` agent - Claude Code groups fine; Codex is the odd one out How it solves it: - Read Codex's unprefixed `session-id` / `thread-id` header - Also the older `session_id` / `conversation_id` spellings - Match the `codex` stem, covering every first-party originator - Gate on the Codex user agent to avoid cross-caller collisions ## User Flow Before: a developer running Codex against the gateway cannot see one Codex session in one place, because every turn is logged as an unrelated request 1. They point Codex at the proxy and run a task that takes five turns 2. Codex sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses five times, each carrying the same conversation uuid in a `session-id` header 3. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and see five separate rows, each stamped with a different, randomly generated session id 4. They filter by the uuid Codex actually used and get zero results, so there is no way to total the cost of that one session After: the same five turns group under the uuid Codex already sends 1. They point Codex at the proxy and run the same five-turn task 2. Codex sends the same five POSTs with the same `session-id` header 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs now shows all five rows sharing one session id 4. Filtering by the uuid Codex used returns all five turns, so the session's cost adds up ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix BEFORE: codex does not return a session id AFTER: codex returns traces under one session id, orphaned traces ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Bare-header path is Codex-only; other clients still need `x-litellm-session-id` - Codex sends `store: false`, so response-id chaining can never group it - Widening the agent match also turns on auto `drop_params` for the Codex TUI ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR --- > [!NOTE] > **Low Risk** > Logging/session-id extraction only, gated on Codex User-Agent and a strict value regex. Widening the agent match also turns on auto drop_params for Codex TUI. > > **Overview** > Codex multi-turn sessions now share one log/session id instead of a fresh per-call trace. > > `get_chain_id_from_headers` now reads Codex’s unprefixed conversation uuid (`session-id` / `thread-id`, plus older `session_id` / `conversation_id`) **only** when the User-Agent is a first-party Codex client. Explicit `x-litellm-*` headers still win. > > `is_codex_user_agent` matches the `codex` stem plus a separator (`codex-tui`, `codex_cli_rs`, `Codex CLI`, etc.) instead of only `codex_`. That also enables auto `drop_params` for the TUI. Unprefixed session headers from non-Codex clients are ignored so traces cannot collide. > > Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 156ec25296b5699d47311d18215a42479df3ec75. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).

signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Embedding and rerank spend never reaches provider budgets - Successful requests emit missing-provider callback errors How it solves it: - Include resolved providers in embedding logging metadata - Include resolved providers in rerank logging metadata ## User Flow Before: a proxy administrator sees successful embedding and rerank requests, but their Bedrock provider budget silently under-counts spend 1. The administrator starts the proxy with Bedrock embedding and rerank models plus a monthly Bedrock provider budget 2. A developer sends `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/embeddings` with model `titan-embed-v2` and receives `200` with an embedding `data` array 3. The proxy logs `ValueError: custom_llm_provider is required`, and `GET http://localhost:4000/provider/budgets` shows no embedding spend increase 4. The developer sends `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/rerank` with model `cohere-rerank-v3-5` and receives `200` with a ranked `results` array 5. The proxy logs the same error, and `GET http://localhost:4000/provider/budgets` shows no rerank spend increase After: the same successful requests are attributed to Bedrock, so the provider budget includes their spend 1. The administrator starts the proxy with the same Bedrock models and monthly provider budget 2. The developer sends the same `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/embeddings` request and receives `200` with an embedding `data` array 3. No missing-provider callback error appears, and `GET http://localhost:4000/provider/budgets` shows increased Bedrock spend 4. The developer sends the same `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/rerank` request and receives `200` with a ranked `results` array 5. No missing-provider callback error appears, and `GET http://localhost:4000/provider/budgets` shows another Bedrock spend increase ## Relevant issues Fixes #37877 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. signals.title: feat(router): per-group supported reasoning efforts with max and ultra levels
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Effort dropdown offers levels many models reject upstream - Nothing tells a caller which efforts a model group takes - The chat to Responses bridge silently drops max today How it solves it: - Model groups report supported_reasoning_efforts, intersected across deployments - Per-level polarity resolved in one module; xhigh, max, ultra are opt-in - The bridge passes any effort level through to the provider ## User Flow Before: an operator wiring reasoning effort into a model group has no way to see which levels a group takes, so a rejected level only surfaces as a provider error at request time 1. They send GET http://localhost:4000/model_group/info with their key and read the entry for gpt-5.6-sol; nothing in it says which reasoning effort levels the group accepts 2. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=models-and-endpoints, Add Model, Auto Router, and the Reasoning effort dropdown offers the same six levels for every model, gpt-5-mini and gpt-5.6-sol alike 3. They pick max for the gpt-5.6-sol tier and the save succeeds with no warning 4. A request routed to that tier goes out as POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `"reasoning_effort": "max"` and comes back 400 `Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'max' with this model. Supported values are: 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'.` 5. They have no way to tell that same level does work on a claude-opus-5 group, so they find out by trying each one After: the group tells the caller exactly which levels it takes, so the level that used to fail upstream is never offered in the first place 1. They send the same GET http://localhost:4000/model_group/info and the gpt-5.6-sol entry now carries `"supported_reasoning_efforts": ["none","low","medium","high","xhigh"]`, gpt-5-mini carries `["minimal","low","medium","high"]`, and a claude-opus-5 group carries all seven up to max 2. Same page, same Add Model flow: gpt-5-mini's dropdown offers Default, minimal, low, medium, high, gpt-5.6-sol offers up to xhigh, and a claude-opus-5 group offers up to max; a group whose deployments intersect to nothing, which one model absent from the model map is enough to cause, keeps the six-level list the dropdown always offered 3. max cannot be picked for the gpt-5.6-sol tier at all, which is the step that used to hand the operator a level the provider then refused 4. A caller who bypasses the picker and sends `"reasoning_effort": "max"` to that group anyway still gets the same provider 400 they got before: the chat-completions gate is unchanged, because litellm converts some chat requests to /v1/responses further down, where max is valid 5. The same level on the claude-opus-5 group still returns 200, and POST http://localhost:4000/v1/responses with `"reasoning": {"effort": "max"}` on gpt-5.6-sol still returns a completed response, so nothing that worked before stops working ## Relevant issues Supersedes #37732, rebuilt on a complete census of every effort-level enumeration site. Design notes: intersection (never any-member) across a group's deployments so routing cannot hand an effort to a deployment that rejects it; polarity mirrors the provider gates (medium/high unconditional, minimal/low opt-out, xhigh/max/ultra opt-in, and none opt-in on azure alone since its gpt-5 config raises without an explicit flag while no other request path refuses the level); gpt-5.6-cyber deliberately gets no effort flags since the map keeps that entry thin, and it carries supports_reasoning true already; the new TypedDict field stays plain like its five siblings, with the repo's writable-ok precedent, because ReadOnly on Pydantic-validated TypedDicts warns; the chat-completions gate keeps owning xhigh alone, since it runs before litellm decides to convert a request to /v1/responses and no map entry asserts the max or ultra flags anyway; deployment model_info is splatted into ModelGroupInfo, so supported_reasoning_efforts validates whatever an operator wrote under that key down to None rather than failing the whole /model_group/info response ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5991 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Two proxies from this repo, one at the merge base and one at the PR tip, on the same config: deployments for `openai/gpt-5-mini`, `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`, `anthropic/claude-opus-5`, `azure/gpt-5-mini`, and `azure/gpt-5.6`, each on live provider credentials. Every call below is a real request against the running proxy with real provider spend, no mocks ### Before (91f2382ab4) #### Group capability advertisement 1. `GET /model_group/info` with the master key 2. No entry carries a `supported_reasoning_efforts` field at all, for any of the five groups #### Chat completions, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 400 litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'max' with this model. Supported values are: 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'.` The level reached the provider before anything caught it #### Chat completions, xhigh on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "xhigh"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'` #### Chat completions, max on a claude-opus-5 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'OK'` #### Responses API, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/responses` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": {"effort": "max"}}` 2. `HTTP 200`, `status=completed` #### Anthropic Messages API, max on both groups 1. `POST /v1/messages` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}`, then the same for `gpt-5.6-sol` 2. `HTTP 200` on both. That surface does not carry reasoning_effort, so the level is dropped before any gating and the gpt-5.6 call succeeds even though the same level fails on chat completions ### After (b7717df9da) #### Group capability advertisement 1. `GET /model_group/info` with the master key 2. Every group carries the field, each one the intersection over its deployments: ``` gpt-5-mini ["minimal", "low", "medium", "high"] gpt-5.6-sol ["none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"] opus-5 ["none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max"] azure-gpt-5-mini ["minimal", "low", "medium", "high"] azure-gpt-5.6 ["none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"] ``` #### Chat completions, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 400 litellm.UnsupportedParamsError: reasoning_effort=max is not supported for this model.` Raised at parameter validation, so no provider call is made and the message names the parameter instead of quoting an upstream error #### Chat completions, xhigh on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "xhigh"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'`, unchanged #### Chat completions, max on a claude-opus-5 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'`, unchanged, and the group advertises max as above #### Responses API, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/responses` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": {"effort": "max"}}` 2. `HTTP 200`, `status=completed`, unchanged #### Anthropic Messages API, max on both groups 1. `POST /v1/messages` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}`, then the same for `gpt-5.6-sol` 2. `HTTP 200` on both, unchanged Observations from the run: - /v1/messages ignores reasoning_effort entirely, before and after - gpt-5.6 takes max on /v1/responses, never on chat - Azure gpt-5 refuses none without an explicit map flag - Advertised sets now match every gate the run exercised ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - gpt-5.6 takes max on /v1/responses but not on chat completions - Chat gating stays on xhigh, so max still fails at the provider - A group that intersects to nothing falls back to every level - Unknown effort strings now reach the provider instead of being dropped - ultra is plumbed everywhere but asserted on no map entry - none resolves as opt-in on azure, opt-out on every other provider ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signals.title: fix(ptu): warn when config.yaml declares PTU while attribution is off
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - PTU in config.yaml accrues nothing while the feature is off - Nothing anywhere says so, so operators assume it is on - A typo drops the deployment with no hint which feature it was How it solves it: - Registration names the declaring deployments once, at startup - The line points at the env var that turns attribution on - Behavior is unchanged: nothing is stripped, rejected, or rescued ## User Flow Before: an admin reserves Azure PTU capacity in config.yaml, and their team's spend never reflects it 1. They add `ptu_count`, `cost_per_ptu_per_hour`, `ptu_effective_from` and `team_id` to a deployment in config.yaml 2. They restart the proxy, which starts cleanly and logs nothing about the reservation 3. They send traffic to that model and it answers normally 4. Days later they open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage, filter to the team, and see only per-token spend; the hourly reservation they configured is nowhere 5. Nothing in the startup log, the model page, or the usage page ever mentioned that the feature was switched off After: the same restart tells them the feature is off and names the variable that turns it on 1. They add the same fields to the same deployment in config.yaml 2. They restart the proxy and the startup log says PTU fields are set on `azure-ptu`, that attribution is disabled so no flat cost accrues and the traffic bills per token, and that `LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION=True` enables it 3. They set that variable and restart; the line is gone 4. They send traffic, and https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=usage now shows the reservation's hourly cost against the team ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Refs LIT-5809 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, both sides. A real Gemini deployment carrying a reservation, alongside an ordinary one, with `LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION` unset: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gemini-ptu litellm_params: model: gemini/gemini-2.5-flash api_key: os.environ/GEMINI_API_KEY model_info: id: gemini-ptu-eastus team_id: team-alpha ptu_count: 100 cost_per_ptu_per_hour: 0.02 ptu_effective_from: "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z" - model_name: gemini-ondemand litellm_params: model: gemini/gemini-2.5-flash api_key: os.environ/GEMINI_API_KEY ``` The typo case reuses the same file with `ptu_count: 0`. Both sides run against the same Postgres, launched with `python -m litellm.proxy.proxy_cli --config <file>` ### Before (4e19127350) #### A reservation declared while attribution is off 1. Start the proxy on the config above, then read the startup log for anything naming PTU: ``` $ grep -ci "PTU cost attribution is disabled" base_valid.log 0 $ grep -i "ptu" base_valid.log | grep -v register_model gemini-ptu ``` 2. The only mention is the deployment's own name in the model list. Nothing says the feature is off 3. The deployment registers and serves: ``` $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4892/model/info -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." | jq -r '.data[] | "\(.model_name) | ptu_count=\(.model_info.ptu_count)"' gemini-ptu | ptu_count=100 gemini-ondemand | ptu_count=null ``` #### A typo in the same reservation 1. Restart on the same file with `ptu_count: 0`, then read the log: ``` $ grep -ci "PTU cost attribution is disabled" base_typo.log 0 $ grep "Error creating deployment" base_typo.log | head -1 19:17:57 - LiteLLM Router:ERROR: router.py:7797 - Error creating deployment: 1 validation error for ModelInfo ``` 2. The deployment is gone, and the error names a pydantic model rather than the feature: ``` $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4892/model/info -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." | jq -r '[.data[].model_name]' ["gemini-ondemand"] ``` ### After (08ca52e846) #### A reservation declared while attribution is off 1. Start the proxy on the same config. The startup log now says so, once: ``` $ grep -c "PTU cost attribution is disabled" flagoff.log 1 $ grep "PTU cost attribution" flagoff.log 19:13:18 - LiteLLM Router:WARNING: router.py:8247 - PTU fields are set on config.yaml deployment(s) gemini-ptu, but PTU cost attribution is disabled, so no flat cost accrues and this traffic is billed per token. Set LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION=True to enable it ``` 2. Only the declaring deployment is named; `gemini-ondemand` is not 3. The deployment registers and serves exactly as before: ``` $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4891/model/info -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." | jq -r '.data[] | "\(.model_name) | id=\(.model_info.id)"' gemini-ptu | id=gemini-ptu-eastus gemini-ondemand | id=76058c439c2182aa7c8fd6a55729eb958321073699bf718f5cc5f7a34bf0d8af ``` 4. A real call through it, on a team key, confirms the line's claim about per-token billing: ``` $ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4891/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-<team key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"gemini-ptu","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with the single word: reserved"}]}' reply: reserved usage: {'completion_tokens': 27, 'prompt_tokens': 8, 'total_tokens': 35} ``` ``` $ psql -tAc "select model_group, spend, ptu_flat_cost is not null from ..." gemini-ptu|6.99e-05 <- billed per token team-alpha|6.99e-05|0 <- LiteLLM_DailyTeamSpend: no flat cost accrued ``` #### The feature switched on 1. Restart with `LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION=True` on the same config: ``` $ grep -c "PTU cost attribution is disabled" flagon.log 0 $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4891/model/info -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." | jq -r '.data[] | "\(.model_name) | ptu_count=\(.model_info.ptu_count)"' gemini-ptu | ptu_count=100 gemini-ondemand | ptu_count=null ``` 2. The line is gone and the deployment is unchanged #### A typo in the same reservation 1. Restart on the `ptu_count: 0` file with attribution still off. Both lines now appear together: ``` $ grep -E "PTU cost attribution is disabled|Error creating deployment" typo.log 19:14:17 - LiteLLM Router:WARNING: router.py:8247 - PTU fields are set on config.yaml deployment(s) gemini-ptu, but PTU cost attribution is disabled, ... 19:14:17 - LiteLLM Router:ERROR: router.py:7799 - Error creating deployment: 1 validation error for ModelInfo ``` 2. The deployment is still dropped, unchanged from base; what is new is that the operator can see which feature the vanished entry belonged to: ``` $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4891/model/info -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." | jq -r '[.data[].model_name]' ["gemini-ondemand"] ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - The typo still drops the deployment; only the silence is fixed - Fires once per Router build, so once per boot or reload - The flag is read only when a config deployment declares PTU ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Low Risk** > Logging-only change on router registration; no billing, auth, or deployment-acceptance behavior is modified. > > **Overview** > Warns at router startup when `config.yaml` deployments set PTU fields while `LITELLM_ENABLE_PTU_COST_ATTRIBUTION` is off, so operators are not left thinking reserved capacity is accruing when traffic is still billed per token. > > Adds `declares_ptu` and logs one warning naming every non-`db_model` declaring deployment (including incomplete or invalid PTU values). Billing and registration are unchanged: nothing is stripped, rejected, or rescued. DB-backed models are skipped because `/model/new` already 400s. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 08ca52e846541ce4c888c8abb69636edaafb3d06. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signals.title: ci: ban row-rewriting DML from prisma migrations
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Migrations apply at proxy boot, so row rewrites are downtime - An unbatched `UPDATE` shipped and had to be reverted - Nothing in CI or the conventions stopped it How it solves it: - New code-quality gate rejects `UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE` in migrations - Also rejects `INSERT ... SELECT` and CTE-led rewrites - Escape-hatch marker must name what bounds the rewrite ## User Flow **Before.** Nothing tells the author their migration rewrites rows, and every proxy that picks up the release stops serving while it runs. 1. An engineer adds a migration that backfills a new column with a single `UPDATE` over the spend logs table, and opens a PR 2. They watch the checks on the PR page. Everything goes green, `code-quality` included, and no check says anything about the migration 3. They get an approval and merge, and the change goes out in the next release 4. An operator upgrades to that release and restarts their proxy 5. Their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` and gets back `500` with `no_db_connection` 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/health/readiness` keeps failing for as long as the rewrite takes, minutes on a large table, then the proxy starts answering on its own with the table's disk usage roughly doubled **After.** The check names the statement and its line before the migration can merge, so the release boots straight into serving traffic. 1. An engineer adds a migration that backfills a new column with a single `UPDATE` over the spend logs table, and opens a PR 2. They watch the checks on the PR page. `code-quality` fails, and its log names the migration file, the line the `UPDATE` sits on, and what to do instead: add the column and let the application backfill it, or move the rewrite to a batched job outside boot 3. They rewrite the migration as plain DDL and push. When the rewrite really is bounded, they put `-- data-migration-ok: <what bounds it>` on the statement instead, and a bare marker with nothing after the colon does not silence the check 4. `code-quality` goes green, they get an approval and merge, and the change goes out in the next release 5. An operator upgrades to that release and restarts their proxy 6. Their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` and gets back `200` with a completion, and `GET https://litellm-domain/health/readiness` answers `200` on the first poll ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This PR adds no runtime surface, so there is no proxy route to curl. The person the change is for is whoever writes the next migration, and what they see is the CI step, so the proof below is that step run from the command line at `73af0e9692`, against trees where fixture migrations have been put on disk. Earlier checkers are compared against by writing them back into the same directory, since the script resolves the repo root from its own location The migration that caused this, restored: ``` $ cat litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260819000000_backfill_spend_log_timestamps/migration.sql -- Backfill created_at/updated_at from endTime for rows written before the columns existed. UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "created_at" = "endTime", "updated_at" = "endTime" WHERE "created_at" > "endTime" + interval '1 hour'; $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260819000000_backfill_spend_log_timestamps/migration.sql:2: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot 1 data-rewriting statement(s) in migrations. Migrations apply at proxy boot, before it serves traffic, so a statement whose cost scales with table size is downtime. Add the column and let the application backfill it, or move the rewrite to a batched job outside boot. If the rewrite is genuinely bounded and has to ship in the migration, mark the statement with the bound spelled out: -- data-migration-ok: <what bounds this> UPDATE ... $ echo $? 1 ``` Every failing run below prints that same guidance block, which the later transcripts drop to stay readable. With a marker that names the bound, the same file passes: ``` $ sed -n '1,3p' litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260819000000_backfill_spend_log_timestamps/migration.sql -- Backfill created_at/updated_at from endTime for rows written before the columns existed. -- data-migration-ok: only rows written before the columns existed, bounded by a one-off window UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 ``` A bare `-- data-migration-ok:` with nothing after the colon does not suppress it, so the hatch cannot be used without saying why the rewrite is safe: ``` $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260819000000_backfill_spend_log_timestamps/migration.sql:3: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The three fixes in `7e6d303e38`, on a fixture holding one of each case: ``` $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000000_spend_log_day_column/migration.sql 1 -- Add the column first. 2 ALTER TABLE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" ADD COLUMN "day" DATE; 3 4 DO $$ 5 BEGIN 6 UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = date_trunc('day', "startTime"); 7 END 8 $$; 9 10 DO $$ 11 BEGIN 12 EXECUTE 'DELETE FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE "startTime" < now() - interval ''90 days'''; 13 END 14 $$; 15 16 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_Config" ("param_name", "param_value") 17 VALUES ('schema_rev', (SELECT max("id")::text FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs")); $ git show 777eb8af10:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_777eb8af10.py $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_777eb8af10.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000000_spend_log_day_column/migration.sql:16: INSERT ... SELECT rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000000_spend_log_day_column/migration.sql:5: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000000_spend_log_day_column/migration.sql:6: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000000_spend_log_day_column/migration.sql:12: DELETE rewrites existing rows at boot ``` All three move: the `UPDATE` was reported on line 5 and is really on line 6, the `DELETE` behind the `EXECUTE` was missed entirely and is now caught on line 12, and the `INSERT ... VALUES` on line 16 is bounded by its literal row list and is no longer called a rewrite Because markers are matched by line, the same line numbering decides which statements a marker covers. Two fixtures, one where a marker sits above an unrelated statement and a real full-table rewrite follows it, one where a marker sits directly above a genuinely bounded rewrite: ``` $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000001_marker_a/migration.sql 1 -- data-migration-ok: one config row, written once at install 2 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_Config" ("param_name", "param_value") VALUES ('schema_rev', '42'); 3 -- the block below is a real full-table rewrite 4 DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = date_trunc('day', "startTime"); END $$; $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000002_marker_b/migration.sql 1 -- Widen the config value column, then fix the one row holding the old schema 2 -- revision. That rewrite is a single row, so it carries a marker. 3 ALTER TABLE "LiteLLM_Config" ALTER COLUMN "param_value" TYPE TEXT; 4 5 ALTER TABLE "LiteLLM_Config" ADD COLUMN "updated_by" TEXT; 6 7 DO $$ 8 BEGIN 9 -- data-migration-ok: single config row, keyed by its primary key 10 UPDATE "LiteLLM_Config" SET "param_value" = '42' WHERE "param_name" = 'schema_rev'; 11 END 12 $$; $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_777eb8af10.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000002_marker_b/migration.sql:6: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000001_marker_a/migration.sql:4: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot ``` The two files swap places, which is the whole bug: the full-table rewrite in `marker_a` was silently exempted by a marker four lines above it that belonged to a different statement, and the properly marked single-row rewrite in `marker_b` was flagged at a line it does not sit on. Both land the right way round now The two fixes in `e7dea842c3` close the ways round the first three. A rewrite parked in a variable and run by name later, and an insert whose only `VALUES` sits behind a set operation, both used to pass: ``` $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000003_dynamic_and_setop/migration.sql 1 DO $$ 2 DECLARE 3 stmt text := 'UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = 1'; 4 BEGIN 5 EXECUTE stmt; 6 END $$; 7 8 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_Config" ("param_name", "param_value") 9 SELECT "k", "v" FROM "Staging" UNION ALL VALUES ('a', 'b'); $ git show 7e6d303e38:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_7e6d303e38.py $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_7e6d303e38.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000003_dynamic_and_setop/migration.sql:8: INSERT ... SELECT rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000003_dynamic_and_setop/migration.sql:3: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The fix in `c4d9a1ac6c` closes the last one. A marker written after the statement it exempts, on the same line, used to hand a free pass to the next statement down as well, and the file went green with no signal anywhere that a full-table rewrite had been let through: ``` $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000004_trailing_marker/migration.sql 1 UPDATE "LiteLLM_Config" SET "param_value" = '2' WHERE "param_name" = 'schema_rev'; -- data-migration-ok: one config row, keyed by its primary key 2 UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = date_trunc('day', "startTime"); $ git show e7dea842c3:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_e7dea842c3.py $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_e7dea842c3.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000004_trailing_marker/migration.sql:2: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The bounded rewrite on line 1 keeps its exemption and the full-table one on line 2 is now flagged, which is the split the file was asking for Dynamic SQL, fixed in `622d9c598d`. Both statements below are correct as written: the first is a single bounded config row carrying a marker, and the second never runs anything at all. The old checker flagged them both, and the only way to silence either was a marker claiming a data migration that was not there: ``` $ git show c4d9a1ac6c:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_c4d9a1ac6c.py $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000005_dynamic_marker_and_inert_text/migration.sql 1 DO $$ 2 BEGIN 3 -- data-migration-ok: one config row, keyed by its primary key 4 EXECUTE ' 5 UPDATE "LiteLLM_Config" SET "param_value" = ''43'' WHERE "param_name" = ''schema_rev'''; 6 END $$; 7 8 DO $$ 9 DECLARE 10 msg text := 'UPDATE of legacy spend rows skipped, the application backfills them'; 11 BEGIN 12 RAISE NOTICE '%', msg; 13 END $$; $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_c4d9a1ac6c.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000005_dynamic_marker_and_inert_text/migration.sql:5: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000005_dynamic_marker_and_inert_text/migration.sql:10: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 ``` The marker now reaches the SQL its `EXECUTE` hands off even though the literal starts a line lower, and a string nothing executes is treated as the message it is. What did not change is the case that matters, a variable that genuinely is executed: ``` $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000006_executed_variable/migration.sql 1 DO $$ 2 DECLARE 3 msg text := 'UPDATE of legacy spend rows skipped'; 4 stmt text := 'DELETE FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE "startTime" < now()'; 5 BEGIN 6 RAISE NOTICE '%', msg; 7 EXECUTE stmt; 8 END $$; $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000006_executed_variable/migration.sql:4: DELETE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The `msg` on line 3 is left alone and the `stmt` on line 4 is still caught, which is the whole distinction One more, fixed in `3cca3f5402`. `DO` takes its body as a string, and dollar quoting is a convenience rather than a requirement, so a body written in single quotes went through untouched: ``` $ git show 622d9c598d:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_622d9c598d.py $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000007_quoted_do_body/migration.sql 1 DO 'BEGIN UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = date_trunc(''day'', "startTime"); END'; 2 3 DO 'BEGIN ALTER TABLE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" ADD COLUMN "week" DATE; END'; $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_622d9c598d.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000007_quoted_do_body/migration.sql:1: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The rewrite on line 1 is caught and the DDL-only block on line 3 is not, so the syntax is scanned rather than merely distrusted Last one, fixed in `3d16e327c6`. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the statement it wraps rather than only planning it, but `ANALYZE` is a statement keyword in its own right, so it stood in for the keyword underneath and the rewrite went through: ``` $ git show 3cca3f5402:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_3cca3f5402.py $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000008_explained_rewrite/migration.sql 1 EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "day" = date_trunc('day', "startTime"); 2 3 EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"; 4 5 ANALYZE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"; $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_3cca3f5402.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000008_explained_rewrite/migration.sql:1: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` Line 1 is caught while the explained `SELECT` on line 3 and the plain `ANALYZE` on line 5 stay quiet, so it is the statement being explained that gets judged, not the wrapper Actually last, fixed in `64267ebd28`. Postgres takes an insert's row source parenthesised, and reading only the unparenthesised text meant a whole-table copy written that way passed. `TABLE t` is a row source too, and it was passing for the same reason: ``` $ git show aabaa5151b:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_aabaa5151b.py $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000009_parenthesised_row_source/migration.sql 1 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_v2" ("request_id", "startTime") 2 (SELECT "request_id", "startTime" FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"); 3 4 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_v3" TABLE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"; 5 6 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_Config" ("param_name", "param_value") 7 VALUES ('schema_rev', (SELECT max("id")::text FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs")); $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_aabaa5151b.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000009_parenthesised_row_source/migration.sql:1: INSERT ... SELECT rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000009_parenthesised_row_source/migration.sql:4: INSERT ... TABLE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` Both copies are caught and the bounded insert on line 6, whose scalar subquery sits in parentheses inside a `VALUES` list, still passes. All three forms were run against a live Postgres 16.14 first to confirm they are valid syntax that really copies rows rather than shapes only the checker cares about: each of them reported `INSERT 0 5` against a five-row source table Two more, fixed in `73af0e9692`. The first is the mirror of the one above: a `VALUES` list bounded the insert even when a set operation joined it to a parenthesised query, which is the same whole-table copy wearing a leading `VALUES`. The second is a rewrite reaching a variable through a query's `INTO` rather than through `:=`, which nothing was reading: ``` $ git show 64267ebd28:tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py > tests/code_coverage_tests/at_64267ebd28.py $ cat -n litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000010_query_backed_and_dynamic_rewrites/migration.sql 1 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_v2" ("request_id") 2 VALUES ('seed') UNION ALL (SELECT "request_id" FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"); 3 4 DO $$ 5 DECLARE 6 stmt text; 7 BEGIN 8 SELECT 'UPDATE "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" SET "session_id" = NULL' INTO stmt; 9 EXECUTE stmt; 10 END $$; 11 12 INSERT INTO "LiteLLM_Config" ("param_name", "param_value") 13 VALUES ('schema_rev', (SELECT max("id")::text FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs")); $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/at_64267ebd28.py No data-rewriting statements in 158 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000010_query_backed_and_dynamic_rewrites/migration.sql:1: INSERT ... SELECT rewrites existing rows at boot litellm-proxy-extras/litellm_proxy_extras/migrations/20260820000010_query_backed_and_dynamic_rewrites/migration.sql:8: UPDATE rewrites existing rows at boot $ echo $? 1 ``` The insert on line 12 still passes, so bounding a list with a scalar subquery in it did not become collateral. Both shapes were run against the same live Postgres 16.14 first: line 1's form reported `INSERT 0 6` copying a five-row table alongside its one literal row, and the block on lines 4 to 10 rewrote all five rows of the target, so each is SQL that runs rather than a shape only the checker cares about After removing the fixtures and the copies of the earlier checkers, against the tree as it ships: ``` $ python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py No data-rewriting statements in 157 migrations. $ echo $? 0 $ git status --porcelain $ echo $? 0 ``` ## Type 🚄 Infrastructure ## Changes Prisma migrations apply synchronously during proxy startup, before the process accepts traffic, so the wall-clock cost of every statement in a migration is startup latency. Schema changes are cheap and bounded. A statement that touches existing rows is not: its cost scales with the table, and on a spend-log-sized table a single `UPDATE` means minutes of a proxy that is up but not serving, plus a heap that has doubled in size and that plain autovacuum will not hand back. We shipped exactly that and had to revert it, and the part worth fixing is that nothing in the repo said not to, so the next person had no way to know `tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py` now walks every `migration.sql` under `litellm-proxy-extras` and fails on any statement whose leading keyword is `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE`, on `INSERT` when its rows come from a query rather than a literal `VALUES` list, and on a CTE-led statement wrapping any of those. `INSERT ... VALUES` passes because the literal row list bounds it. The check runs in the existing Code Quality job, which has no path filter, so a migration that arrives through a rebase or a merge is still gated, and it costs nothing extra since that job already runs on every PR Getting this right on real SQL took more than a grep. `ON DELETE CASCADE` and `ON UPDATE CASCADE` appear 60 times across the current migrations and are schema, never a statement's leading keyword, so the checker resolves each statement's own keyword instead of matching anywhere in the text. `DO $$ ... $$` is this repo's idiom for conditional DDL and appears 11 times, so dollar-quoted bodies are scanned recursively and PL/pgSQL block syntax is transparent to the keyword lookup, which also means an `IF EXISTS (...)` guard cannot stand in for the statement it guards. Comments, single-quoted strings, double-quoted identifiers and dollar-quoted bodies are masked in place before parsing, keeping every offset where it was Three things the first pass got wrong, fixed in `7e6d303e38`. Line numbers inside a dollar-quoted body were counted against the sliced body text while the offset into it stayed absolute, so a statement inside a `DO $$ ... $$` block reported a line it does not sit on. Since the escape-hatch markers are matched by line, that same slip cut both ways: an unrelated marker earlier in the file silently exempted a real full-table rewrite, and a marker sitting directly above a bounded one failed to exempt it. Scanning now threads each region's offset through and counts lines against the whole file, however deeply the statement is nested. Second, `EXECUTE 'UPDATE ...'` passed, because the DML sat inside a string literal that masking had already blanked, so the literals an `EXECUTE` runs are now scanned as SQL in their own right; a rewrite reads the same to Postgres whether it is spelled out or handed over as a string. Third, an `INSERT ... VALUES` carrying a scalar subquery in its value list was flagged as an `INSERT ... SELECT`. A top-level `VALUES` bounds the insert to the rows written out there, so the parenthesised subqueries and helper CTEs around it no longer make it a rewrite Two ways round those, closed in `e7dea842c3`. A rewrite can be parked in a variable and run by name a few lines later, where the literal sits outside the `EXECUTE` statement and nothing scanned it, so a literal assigned with `:=` is now read as SQL just like one an `EXECUTE` holds directly. And bounding an insert on the presence of a top-level `VALUES` was too generous, since a `VALUES` reached through a set operation bounds nothing; what decides it now is whether the insert is built on a `SELECT` of its own, which also keeps the scalar subqueries in a `VALUES` list out of it because those sit in parentheses. Both directions err towards flagging, which is the right way to be wrong here: a false positive costs a marker naming the bound, a false negative costs a proxy that boots into a table rewrite Which statement a marker speaks for is its own question, settled in `c4d9a1ac6c`. A marker written on a line of its own speaks for the statement below it, which is how one placed above a rewrite exempts it, and a marker sharing a line with the statement it follows speaks for that statement alone. The old rule looked one line up unconditionally, so writing the marker inline at the end of a statement, a perfectly natural style, quietly exempted the next statement too, and nothing anywhere went red to say so. That was the worst shape a bug in this checker can take, since the whole point of the gate is that a rewrite cannot reach a boot unnoticed Dynamic SQL needed two more corrections, in `622d9c598d`. A marker written above an `EXECUTE` did not reach the SQL that `EXECUTE` runs once the literal's first line sat below it, so the documented placement failed CI and the only way to silence it was to bury the marker inside the string being executed. A marker on an `EXECUTE`, or on the assignment feeding one, now covers what that statement hands off. The other way round, a literal assigned with `:=` was read as SQL whether or not anything ran it, so an error message that happens to begin with the word `UPDATE` was reported as a data migration. A literal now counts only when an `EXECUTE` in the same body runs that variable by name. That direction matters more than it looks: the only way to quiet a false positive is a marker, and a marker on a statement that is not a data migration at all is a lie that erodes what every other marker means One more gap, closed in `3cca3f5402`. `DO` takes its body as a string literal, and dollar quoting is a convenience rather than a requirement, so a migration spelling the body in single quotes got its rewrite through completely untouched. That is ordinary syntax rather than an attempt to hide anything, which makes it reachable by accident, and it is the shape this whole check exists to stop. Quoted `DO` bodies are now scanned like any other SQL a statement hands to the server One last gap, closed in `3d16e327c6`. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the statement it wraps rather than only planning it, so a rewrite underneath one rewrites the table for real on the way to printing its timings. `ANALYZE` is a statement keyword of its own, though, and it sits ahead of the rewrite, so it was being read as the statement's keyword and the rewrite passed. An `EXPLAIN` is now transparent and the statement being explained is what gets judged. The old behaviour was worse than a plain miss, because it had the two cases exactly backwards: `EXPLAIN UPDATE`, which only plans, was flagged, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE`, which runs, was not. Both are flagged now, since nothing here needs the plan of a statement it is being told not to run at boot The last gap, closed in `64267ebd28`, is one this PR introduced itself and is worth tracing because the two halves of it pull in opposite directions. Postgres accepts an insert's row source wrapped in parentheses, so `INSERT INTO "t" ("a") (SELECT ...)` copies a whole table. `777eb8af10` caught that shape by looking for a `SELECT` anywhere in the statement, but that also flagged a scalar subquery sitting in a `VALUES` list. `7e6d303e38` bounded it on a top-level `VALUES`, and `e7dea842c3` replaced that with a `SELECT` read only outside parentheses, which fixed a `VALUES` joined to a query by a set operation and traded the parenthesised form away in the same move. What was missing is that these are two questions rather than one: a query outside every parenthesis is the row source outright, and only when there is none does a top-level `VALUES` get to bound the insert, with a parenthesised query counting when neither applies. All three shapes hold now. `TABLE t` is a row source as much as a `SELECT` is and was passing for the same reason, so it is read as one too, which is safe because double-quoted identifiers are masked before this runs and the bare word can only be syntax. Every form was checked against a live Postgres 16.14 before being called a miss, since a checker gap only matters if the SQL it lets through actually runs `73af0e9692` closes the mirror image of that gap and one next to it. Reading the row source outside parentheses first meant a `VALUES` list still bounded an insert when a set operation joined it to a parenthesised query, so `VALUES (1) UNION ALL (SELECT ...)` copied a whole table with a literal row in front of it. A `VALUES` list now bounds an insert only while no set operation sits beside it at that same level, and a set operation nested inside the list is not beside it, so a subquery with its own `UNION` in it still passes. The second gap is on the dynamic-SQL side: PL/pgSQL parks a string in a variable through a query's `INTO` and through the bare `=` it accepts as the assignment operator, and only `:=` was being read, so a rewrite handed to a later `EXECUTE` went unseen either way. `INTO` is unambiguous and simply counts. A bare `=` is comparison to the rest of SQL, so it names a target only where the words ahead of it are a name and perhaps a type rather than a statement keyword or a word guarding a condition, and those guards stop counting once a `THEN` or an `ELSE` ends the condition they opened. That keeps `IF stmt = 'DELETE FROM ...'` reading as the test it is while catching the assignment written on the same line as the `IF` that opened the block One decision worth naming, since it looks like a gap and is not. A marker on an `EXECUTE` covers a single-quoted payload, because that payload is an opaque string the statement hands to the server. A dollar-quoted payload is not treated as a string at all but as a region read like any other body, so a rewrite inside one carries its own marker, on the rewrite itself, which is also what the failure guidance prints. Making a marker cover a whole dollar-quoted body would read as more consistent and would be a real hole: `DO $$ ... $$` is this repo's idiom for conditional DDL, used by 11 of the 157 migrations on disk, and one marker on the block header would then silence every rewrite inside it, including one added months later by someone who never saw the marker. The current behaviour fails loudly and costs a marker in the right place; the alternative fails silently and costs a proxy booting into a table rewrite. Four tests pin it, and all four fail if the exemption is widened that way Where this stops is written down rather than left to be discovered. Each literal is read on its own, so a keyword assembled by concatenating fragments that do not contain it, `'UPD' || 'ATE ...'`, is not caught. Every fragment is scanned, so a concatenation is caught wherever the keyword survives whole in one of them, which covers `'UPDATE ' || quote_ident(t)` and the rest of the shapes anyone actually writes. Reaching the gap takes a keyword deliberately split down the middle, and this is a guard against a rewrite reaching a boot unnoticed, not a defence against someone hiding one on purpose Two migrations already on disk contain an `UPDATE`. Prisma checksums applied migration files and the repo treats them as immutable, so neither can carry an inline marker. They sit in a closed `GRANDFATHERED` set instead, and the checker fails if either one stops violating or disappears, which keeps the baseline from quietly going vacuous The rule itself is written down in `CLAUDE.md` next to the other conventions, since a gate that fails without explaining the alternative just gets worked around On tests: 124 cases, and I mutation-tested the checker rather than trusting the count. The first pass killed 12 of 18 mutants, and every survivor was a test that named the right feature but picked an input where the feature's absence was masked by the keyword lookup landing on a different, still-harmless keyword. A later commit fixes that, so all 17 killable mutants now die. The eighteenth turned out to be an equivalent mutant: the doubled-quote branch in `skip_quoted` masked the same span whether or not it was there, verified exhaustively over every input up to length 6 in the relevant alphabet, so that branch is gone rather than left as untestable code. The 76 cases added since then cover dynamic SQL, bounded and query-backed inserts, marker placement and its scope inside dollar-quoted regions, quoted `DO` bodies, explained statements, and line numbering under nesting. Run against the earlier checkers, 35 of the 124 fail at `777eb8af10`, 25 at `7e6d303e38`, 29 at `e7dea842c3`, 27 at `c4d9a1ac6c`, 21 at `622d9c598d`, 19 at `3cca3f5402`, 15 at `3d16e327c6`, 15 at `aabaa5151b` and 8 at `64267ebd28`, so they pin real regressions instead of restating what already worked. Two things in that sequence are worth reading. It does not fall monotonically, and the step up at `e7dea842c3` is the parenthesised row source `64267ebd28` closes, with cases that pass at `7e6d303e38` and fail from `e7dea842c3` onwards, which is the suite naming the commit that introduced the gap rather than only the one that fixed it. And `aabaa5151b` ties `3d16e327c6` exactly, which is the same non-behavioural claim its checklist line makes, arrived at from the other direction ## Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- devin-review-badge-begin --> --- <a href="https://app.devin.ai/review/berriai/litellm/pull/37899" target="_blank"> <picture> <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://static.devin.ai/assets/gh-open-in-devin-review-dark.svg?v=1"> <img src="https://static.devin.ai/assets/gh-open-in-devin-review-light.svg?v=1" alt="Open in Devin Review"> </picture> </a> <!-- devin-review-badge-end --> - [x] c4d9a1ac6c passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 622d9c598d passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 3cca3f5402 passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 3d16e327c6 passes /live-pr-risk - [x] aabaa5151b is non-behavioural against `3d16e327c6`: a docstring, six tests, and one helper reuse, with 0 scan differences across all 157 migrations on disk and all 51 SQL shapes in the suite - [x] 64267ebd28 passes /live-pr-risk. Nothing here is imported by the proxy, so the dependency graph closes inside the one file: the renamed helper has no reference outside it, the suite loads the checker by path rather than by symbol, and the keyword string it reports has no consumer anywhere. The entrypoint is the CI step, run verbatim as `uv run --no-sync python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py`, exit 0 in 0.14s over the 157 shipped migrations. Also run on the tree merged into current `litellm_internal_staging` (`4e19127350`), which merges cleanly: exit 0 there too, and 113/113 tests pass, so the new gate does not fail on a migration that landed while this sat open - [x] 73af0e9692 passes /live-pr-risk. The commit adds five names and rewrites two helpers, and the graph closes inside the one file exactly as before: `assigns_rather_than_compares`, `GUARDS_A_CONDITION`, `OPENS_A_BLOCK`, `INTO_TARGETS` and `JOINS_QUERIES` have zero references outside the checker, as do the two helpers whose bodies changed, the suite still loads the checker by path rather than by symbol, and the reported keyword string still has no consumer. The entrypoint is the CI step, run verbatim as `uv run --no-sync python ./tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py`, exit 0 in 0.09s over the 157 shipped migrations, so neither the widened `INSERT` rule nor the widened assignment rule fires on anything already on disk. Also run on the tree merged into current `litellm_internal_staging` (`4e19127350`), which merges cleanly: exit 0 there too, and 124/124 tests pass

signals.title: fix(mcp): resolve admin OAuth sessions to the same server set the connect page shows
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - An admin who SSO's into the gateway during an MCP OAuth connect flow gets a session that resolves zero MCP servers unless they are explicitly granted each one, so Claude Code shows "connected" with no tools (silently on older builds, as an access_denied since #37865) while the dashboard shows them every server. Reported by a customer on v1.96.2 - The cause is two resolvers answering "which servers can this human reach": the dashboard list applies the admin view shortcut, and the OAuth-admitted subject path deliberately skips it (`not is_admitted_subject` in `MCPServerManager.get_allowed_mcp_servers`). The restriction is vacuous against an admin, who can self-grant or paste an admin virtual key and get the registry anyway, so it only produces the mismatch How it solves it: - One predicate now owns the admin-view question for both credential shapes: `MCPRequestHandler.admin_view_unscoped` returns True for an admin-view role with no explicit `object_permission.mcp_servers` scope and no entitlement ceiling, and both the server-axis registry resolution and the tools-axis open channel call it, for keys and admitted session subjects alike - The registry result is seeded into the union instead of returned early, so the RFC 8707 session resource scope still bounds a per-server envelope held by an admin (the old early return would have widened it) - On the tools axis, admin view joins the existing open-channel arm riding the user's OWN source, so registry servers are invokable rather than listable but uninvokable. An admin whose user row carries any entitlement never reaches the channel because the ceiling clause disqualifies the predicate first - Non-admins are unchanged: their session already resolves their own connect-page set, and the #37865 access_denied at authorize still fires for them. A key's explicit object_permission scope still wins even for admins, empty list included. An admitted subject's object_permission is the user's own row, whose mcp_servers column is [] by DB default, so for that shape the row binds through the entitlement ceiling instead (any non-empty entitlement disqualifies the registry seed), the same reading operator_open_server_ids already applies to that row - In-scope servers the gateway holds no upstream credential for already surface as `{"status": "auth_required"}` in the tools/list `_meta` server outcomes, so nothing on that axis needed code This supersedes the design direction of open PR #34585, which locks UI sessions to the admitted-subject resolver with no admin registry path ## Relevant issues - #36358: the silent no-tools symptom for bridge-admitted users came from this scope filter; #37865 made it loud, this PR makes it not fire for users whose dashboard shows the server - #34585 (open): rewires dashboard sessions into the admitted-subject resolver, the opposite direction from this change ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Rig: proxy from this branch on localhost:4612 with real Postgres, one stub upstream MCP server on :8933 that 401s without its bearer and counts authenticated requests, and a stub IdP on :8934. Two servers registered with `allow_all_keys: false` and zero grants: `cust_bridge` (oauth_delegate + dcr_bridge) and `cust_oauth2` (oauth2, authorization_code). The change is on the auth path, so no LLM call is involved; the upstream MCP server is a local stub per the established precedent for request-path changes (#30277, #34029) Before (base commit, same commands): the admin's dashboard `GET /v1/mcp/server` lists both servers, `?connected_app_view=true` marks both `connected_app_reachable: false` (empty connect picker), and the DCR walk dies at authorize ``` REACHED CLIENT CALLBACK: http://127.0.0.1:9777/callback?error=access_denied&error_description=the+signed-in+user+has+no+access+to+MCP+server+%27cust_bridge%27... ``` After (this branch), same admin, fresh session: ``` $ curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4612/v1/mcp/server?connected_app_view=true" -H "Authorization: Bearer $UI_SESSION_KEY" cust_bridge | connected_app_reachable: True cust_oauth2 | connected_app_reachable: True $ SERVER=cust_bridge ./repro_walk.sh # DCR register -> authorize -> token -> MCP initialize -> tools/list initialize -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK tools/list -> {"_meta":{"litellm.ai/server_outcomes":{"cust_bridge":{"status":"ok","tool_count":1}}},"tools":[{"name":"cust_bridge-echo",...}]} $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8933/stats # stub upstream authed_requests went 40 -> 43 with the injected bearer {"authed_requests": 43, ..., "last_auth_header": "Bearer real_upstream_token_12345"} ``` Non-admin negative control (fresh internal_user session, same walk) still denies loudly: ``` location: http://127.0.0.1:9777/callback?error=access_denied&error_description=the+signed-in+user+has+no+access... ``` Explicit scope still wins: after `POST /user/update` with `object_permission.mcp_servers = [cust_oauth2_id]`, a fresh admin session resolves only that server. And in-scope servers with no upstream credential surface in `_meta` instead of vanishing: ``` outcomes: {"cust_bridge": {"status": "auth_required", "http_status": 401}, "cust_oauth2": {"status": "auth_required", "http_status": 401}} ``` ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/auth/user_api_key_auth_mcp.py`: new `MCPRequestHandler.admin_view_unscoped` predicate (the one owner of the admin-view question), and `_resolve_admitted_subject_tools` treats it as an open channel riding the user's own source `litellm/proxy/_experimental/mcp_server/mcp_server_manager.py`: `get_allowed_mcp_servers` replaces the inline four-clause admin arm and its `not is_admitted_subject` carve-out with the shared predicate, seeding the registry into the union so the session resource scope bounds every return Tests: the old pin `test_admitted_admin_is_scoped_to_grants_not_full_registry` is rewritten to the new invariant (parametrized over PROXY_ADMIN and PROXY_ADMIN_VIEW_ONLY, asserting session equals key view), plus new pins for explicit key scope, unresolved entitlement ceiling, the tools-axis channel with a non-admin negative, the registry seed bounded by a sealed session resource scope, the DB-default empty mcp_servers row still resolving the registry, and a non-admin admitted subject never getting the registry. Each fails on the commit before the code it pins Second commit (179e5819, from review): the credential scope clause in `admin_view_unscoped` applies only to non-admitted principals, so an admitted admin whose shared permission row exists with the DB-default empty mcp_servers list still resolves the registry, verified live on the rig (connect view flips to reachable True with the [] row in place) ## QA runbook 1. Start a proxy from this branch with a Postgres DATABASE_URL and `store_model_in_db: true`, master key `sk-1234` 2. Register an MCP server with `allow_all_keys: false` and no grants (any oauth_delegate + dcr_bridge server works; a stub works too) 3. Log into the UI as the master admin, open the connect flow (`/ui/connect?connect_flow=1` or via Claude Code pointing at `https://<proxy>/<server>/mcp`), and confirm the server now shows as connectable 4. Complete the OAuth flow from Claude Code and run a tool: tools list and serve without any object permission grant 5. Create an `internal_user`, sign in as them, repeat step 4, and confirm the authorize step still redirects with `error=access_denied` 6. Grant the admin an explicit `object_permission.mcp_servers` list and confirm a fresh session resolves only those servers ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signals.title: test: say whether a match= pattern is a regex or a literal (ruff RUF043)
signals.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - `match=` is `re.search`, so a copied `.` is a wildcard - The block then accepts messages nobody meant to accept - 25 such patterns, and nothing stops the next one How it solves it: - Selects ruff `RUF043` in `ruff-tests.toml`, already wired to CI - A real regex gets an `r` prefix, so the intent is on the page - A literal message gets `re.escape`, so every character means itself - One `\.` where a literal dot sat inside a real regex ## User Flow Before: an operator who declares a PTU reservation can have the field name change under them, because the test guarding the message passes either way 1. They add a deployment to config.yaml with PTU fields set and no `model_info.id` 2. The proxy refuses to start and says `model_info.id is required when PTU fields are set` 3. They add `model_info: {id: ...}` and the deployment comes up billing under the id they own 4. Someone renames the field in that message to `model_info_id`, and CI stays green, because the test pinning the message reads the dot as "any character" 5. The next operator copies `model_info.id` out of the docs, the proxy does not recognise it, and their reservation bills under a hash of the credential instead After: the message cannot drift without CI going red 1. The same rename is made 2. The test fails, because the pattern now demands the field name exactly as written 3. The message and the docs keep naming the same field, so the operator's reservation stays under one identity ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This PR changes lint config and tests, so there is no proxy route to curl. What matters for a rule that claims to catch patterns which accept the wrong message is whether one of them actually does, so a message a test pins is renamed and the test is run on both sides. The mutation: in `litellm/litellm_core_utils/ptu_pricing.py`, the refusal `"model_info.id is required when PTU fields are set..."` is renamed to `"model_info_id is required..."`. The test pins that message with `match="model_info.id is required"`, where the dot matches the underscore. ### Before (66b930b540) 1. Run ``` pytest "tests/test_litellm/test_router_model_cost_isolation.py::test_a_reservation_without_a_declared_id_is_refused" ``` 2. Output: ``` 1 passed, 1 warning in 0.18s ``` The field named in the error is no longer the field the docs name, and the test that pins it still passes. ### After (91599aef69) 1. Run ``` pytest "tests/test_litellm/test_router_model_cost_isolation.py::test_a_reservation_without_a_declared_id_is_refused" ``` 2. Output: ``` FAILED tests/test_litellm/test_router_model_cost_isolation.py::test_a_reservation_without_a_declared_id_is_refused 1 failed, 1 warning in 0.19s ``` 3. Run ``` ruff check --config ruff-tests.toml tests ``` 4. Output: ``` All checks passed! ``` ### Rule and regression numbers `ruff check --config ruff-tests.toml tests` went from 25 `RUF043` findings to zero. Running the touched files that need neither network nor a database gives the same tally on both sides, 1113 passed and 140 errors, every error pre-existing and all of them one fixture the router helper module cannot build here. Thirteen patterns were deliberate regexes and only needed marking raw, eleven were the message itself and now go through `re.escape`, and one had a literal dot sitting inside a real regex, so only that dot is escaped. The first commit is separate on purpose: the `match=` literals PR #37887 minted carry the same hazard, and they are escaped before the rule that would have caught them turns on. ## Type 🧹 Refactoring 🚄 Infrastructure ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - `re.escape` makes trailing periods literal, so each message was read first - A raw prefix silences the rule without narrowing a genuinely broad `.*` ### Final Attestation - [ ] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR
