signal.title: fix(websearch_interception): end the turn when the agentic loop hits its ceiling
signal.text: ## TLDR When the web search interception loop hits its ceiling, `/v1/messages` now ends the turn cleanly instead of handing the client a `tool_use` block for `litellm_web_search`, an internal tool the client never declared and has no way to answer. Also adds a `max_agentic_loops` setting to `websearch_interception_params` ## User Flow **Before** The turn comes back carrying a tool call the app never asked for, so it has nothing to answer with and the conversation dead-ends. 1. A developer runs a LiteLLM proxy with web search interception turned on for their Bedrock Claude models, pointed at their search provider. They try to raise the search loop's ceiling with `max_agentic_loops: 5` under `litellm_settings.websearch_interception_params`; the proxy starts fine and the key does nothing, so the ceiling stays at the default of 3 unless they repeat it under every model's `litellm_params` 2. From an internal research app built on Anthropic's Python SDK (`client.messages.create`, no streaming) and pointed at the proxy, they ask a question that needs several rounds of searching, something like "compare current on-demand H100 pricing at the three biggest cloud providers and tell me which is cheapest" 3. The app sends `POST https://litellm-proxy/v1/messages` with `"model": "claude-sonnet-4-5"`, no `stream`, and `"tools": [{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search"}]` 4. The proxy runs the searches on their behalf and asks the model again after each round, up to 3 rounds 5. The model asks for one more search after the last allowed round 6. `HTTP 200` comes back with `"stop_reason": "tool_use"` and a content block `{"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01...", "name": "litellm_web_search", "input": {"query": "..."}}` 7. The app has no tool by that name. It declared Anthropic's `web_search` and nothing else, so there is nothing to run and no result to hand back, and the person waiting on the answer gets none 8. The developer appends that assistant turn and sends the next `POST https://litellm-proxy/v1/messages` anyway, and gets `HTTP 400` because the `tool_use` block has no matching `tool_result`. The only way forward is to throw the turn away and start the conversation over **After** The turn comes back finished, the app renders the answer, and the next message goes through. 1. Same setup, except `max_agentic_loops: 5` under `litellm_settings.websearch_interception_params` now applies to every intercepted model, and a value the loop cannot honor (`0`, `-1`, `"five"`, `true`) stops the proxy at startup with a message naming the key instead of being quietly ignored. A per model `litellm_params.max_agentic_loops` still wins where it is set 2. The same question from the same app 3. The same `POST https://litellm-proxy/v1/messages` request 4. The proxy runs the searches on their behalf and asks the model again after each round, up to the ceiling 5. The model asks for one more search after the last allowed round 6. `HTTP 200` comes back with `"stop_reason": "end_turn"`, the text and web search result blocks the turn produced, and no block named `litellm_web_search` anywhere in the body 7. The app renders the answer. It can be thinner than it would have been with more rounds, since the searching stopped at the ceiling, and `max_agentic_loops` is the knob for that 8. The developer sends their follow-up `POST https://litellm-proxy/v1/messages` with that assistant turn in the history and gets `HTTP 200`. The conversation carries on ## What was happening `_check_agentic_loop_safety` raised a `ValueError` when the loop ceiling or the repeated tool-call fingerprint guard tripped. That raise crossed the parent frame's unguarded `await anthropic_messages.acreate(...)` in `_execute_anthropic_agentic_plan`, so the parent's `async_post_agentic_loop_response_hook` never ran, and one frame further up an `except Exception` swallowed it and logged `LiteLLM.AgenticHookError`. The response that then fell through to the client was the raw model turn, internal `tool_use` block and all ## The fix `_check_agentic_loop_safety` now raises `AgenticLoopSafetyError`, which subclasses `ValueError` so anything already catching the broader type keeps working. `_call_agentic_completion_hooks` catches that specific type and returns a finalized response: the blocks for the tool calls the rail just refused are dropped, and if nothing the client declared is left waiting, `stop_reason` is closed out. It returns through `_maybe_wrap_in_fake_stream` like every other path there, so a converted stream still gets a stream back. The refused blocks are matched by the ids and names of the tool calls the safety check refused rather than by hardcoding `litellm_web_search`, since this machinery is not web search specific. A block that carries an id is matched on the id alone, so a tool the client declared under the same name as a refused one is left alone The terminal response only replaces the turn on the non-streaming `/v1/messages` path, which is where the bug was reported and which includes a streaming client whose request the interceptor converted. The two other callers keep raising exactly as they do today. A genuinely streaming caller has already sent the original message to the client by the time the hooks run, so a finalized turn would arrive as a second `message_start` through `message_stop` rather than replace the first one, and I measured that duplicate before scoping it. The responses surface hands this code a pydantic model rather than the Anthropic dict the finalizer rewrites, so returning it would turn a loud failure into a quiet 200 that still carries the internal call. Both are worth fixing and neither is fixable here One decision worth pushing back on if you disagree: the terminal `stop_reason` is `end_turn`. The type at `litellm/types/llms/anthropic_messages/anthropic_response.py` is `Literal["end_turn", "max_tokens", "stop_sequence", "tool_use"] | None`, so there is no truncation value to use, and inventing a new string breaks the type and strict SDK clients. `end_turn` is also what the real Anthropic API returns for the same question when its own server side web search stops calling tools. `max_tokens` was the alternative and it would be a lie: nothing hit a token limit, and clients that auto-continue on `max_tokens` would start a pointless follow-up turn ## The knob `max_agentic_loops` is now readable from `litellm_settings.websearch_interception_params`, so the ceiling can be set for the feature as a whole. The interceptor injects it from its pre-request hook, which runs on `/v1/messages`, so that is the surface it covers. The per deployment setting below is the one that applies wherever the loop runs: ```yaml litellm_settings: callbacks: ["websearch_interception"] websearch_interception_params: enabled_providers: ["bedrock"] search_tool_name: "my-tavily-search" max_agentic_loops: 5 ``` To be clear about what this adds: a per deployment `litellm_params.max_agentic_loops` already worked before this PR and still wins over the feature-level setting, so this is a convenience for operators who want one ceiling for every intercepted model rather than a new capability. `max_agentic_loops` stays on the proxy's untrusted root field list, so a client still cannot raise its own ceiling from the request body A value that the loop cannot honor (zero, negative, a string, a bool) is rejected when the config is read rather than quietly ignored. That is stricter than the rest of this handler, which tends to coerce and fall back, so it is easy to soften if reviewers prefer. It can only fire on a config that sets the new key ## Not in this PR - The chat completions sibling loop in `litellm/litellm_core_utils/chat_completion_agentic_loop.py` leaks the same way. PR #37657 is editing that file right now, so it is a follow-up rather than a conflict - A genuinely streaming request, meaning one the interceptor did not convert, still leaks the internal `tool_use` block, because the message is on the wire before the cap is even checked. Ending that turn cleanly means catching the rail before the first message is sent rather than after, which is a bigger change to the streaming iterator than this fix should carry - The responses surface still returns a 500 when a rail trips. Giving it the same treatment means teaching the finalizer the responses shape, which is worth doing on its own rather than inside a `/v1/messages` fix - When the refused block was the only thing in the turn, the client gets `end_turn` with empty content instead of text saying the search was cut short. That is recoverable where the old behavior was not, but it is thin, and writing assistant text on the model's behalf felt like a product call rather than a bug fix - On a multi hop search, only the outermost loop injects the native `server_tool_use` and `web_search_tool_result` blocks, because the follow-up kwargs strip the flag that turns them on. This fix restores the post-loop hook run on the frame that was being skipped, but it does not make every executed search show up in the response. That gap is being tracked separately - The fake Anthropic stream iterator only emits `content_block_start` for `text`, `thinking`, `redacted_thinking` and `tool_use`, while it emits `content_block_stop` for every block, so `server_tool_use` and `web_search_tool_result` come out as an orphan stop with no start. That is tracked separately, and it matters here: on a capped streaming turn the internal tool call is now gone and those two blocks are the only ones left, so the client sees a terminal stream with no content in it. The turn is at least terminal and recoverable, where before it was neither, but the streaming client still gets less than the non-streaming one until that iterator is fixed. The blocks themselves do survive the cap, which is what the orphan stops at index 0 and 1 show, so this is presentation and not data loss - The capped streaming path is not cost attributed, while the identical non-streaming request is, also tracked separately - The Anthropic agentic path never runs `_run_agentic_loop_cleanup`, where the Responses path does. That is pre-existing and not specific to the ceiling, so changing it would move behavior for every intercepted anthropic request ## Testing New unit tests in `tests/test_litellm/integrations/websearch_interception/test_websearch_agentic_loop_cap.py` cover the capped response being terminal, the same for the repeated fingerprint guard, no follow-up call being planned once a rail trips, the caller's response not being mutated, a client declared `tool_use` surviving with `stop_reason` left alone, only the refused tool calls being dropped when a client declares a tool of the same name, tool calls without ids still matching by name, a non-dict response passing through untouched, the converted stream still getting a terminal fake stream, the streaming and responses callers still raising, the parent frame's post-loop hook running and its blocks landing, and the new knob from config through to the loop settings including precedence and rejected values Verified live as well, on a proxy against the real Anthropic API with a real search backend and `max_agentic_loops: 2` set through the new setting, using a prompt that forces one search per turn so the loop actually chains. The proxy logged `LiteLLM.AgenticLoopRefused: ending turn ... Exceeded max_agentic_loops=2` once per capped request and no `AgenticHookError` at all, where before the fix that same request logged `AgenticHookError`. It returned: - non-streaming: HTTP 200, `stop_reason: end_turn`, blocks `['server_tool_use', 'web_search_tool_result']`, no `tool_use` block, and the string `litellm_web_search` nowhere in the body. On the same request before the fix: blocks `['server_tool_use', 'web_search_tool_result', 'text', 'tool_use']` with `stop_reason: tool_use` and the internal tool name in the body - streaming: HTTP 200, `stop_reason: end_turn` in `message_delta`, clean `message_stop`, no `content_block_start` naming the internal tool - below the ceiling: unchanged, one search, `end_turn`, citations present, and a correct answer

signal.title: fix(files): list and page unscoped managed files locally
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Unscoped file lists default to unauthenticated OpenAI calls - Managed files become unavailable without OpenAI credentials - Files the caller owns go missing whenever the provider's page does not carry them, even though the same ids still retrieve - `limit` and `after` are accepted and silently ignored, and `has_more` is always false, so a client that pages until `has_more` is false stops after one page and concludes it has seen everything How it solves it: - Read owner-scoped managed rows for unscoped requests - Page those rows with a keyset cursor on `unified_file_id`, so a key that owns every file on the proxy still reads one bounded page at a time - Accept `limit` and `after` on the route and report an honest `has_more` - Never return an empty page while matching rows remain, so `has_more` false always means the caller has seen everything and an SDK that pages off the last item cannot stop early - Reject a `limit` outside the documented range with a 400 that names the parameter - Preserve explicit provider and model listing behavior `limit` follows what OpenAI documents for `GET /v1/files`: 1 to 10000, default 10000. That keeps the listing OpenAI-compatible and does not shrink the page for anyone who never paged before. ## User Flow Before: a developer listing gateway-managed files depends on an OpenAI account they may not have, and cannot page 1. They send GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files with their proxy key 2. They provide no provider or target model because the files are gateway-managed 3. The proxy calls OpenAI on their behalf, so the request fails with a missing credentials error when the proxy has no OpenAI account 4. Where credentials do exist, the response only carries the managed files whose provider-side file happened to be on the page OpenAI returned, so files they own and can still read with GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files/{file_id} are missing from the list 5. They retry with ?limit=2 and every file comes back anyway 6. They retry with ?after={the last id they saw} and the same first page comes back, with `has_more` false 7. They pass an ?after= id that cannot exist and get 200 with the full page, so a bad cursor is indistinguishable from a good one After: the same request lists every file the caller owns, one page at a time 1. They send GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files with their proxy key and no provider or target model 2. The response is 200 with every file they own, newest first, using ids that work on GET https://litellm-domain/v1/files/{file_id} 3. No OpenAI account is needed and no upstream provider call is made 4. They retry with ?limit=2 and get two files, with `has_more` true 5. They retry with ?after={last_id}&limit=2 and get the next two files, with no overlap, and keep going until `has_more` is false 6. They add ?purpose=batch to narrow the listing to their batch inputs, and every page comes back filled with matches however small their ?limit= is, so iterating with their SDK reaches every one 7. An ?after= id they do not own returns 400, so the cursor cannot be used to probe another caller's files 8. A ?limit= outside 1 to 10000 returns 400 naming the parameter on every shape of the route, whether or not they pin a model, so their SDK surfaces it instead of retrying a server error ## Relevant issues Fixes #37714 Refs #35362 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The relevant test files pass locally with 116 passed and 2 skipped, and the two directories they live in pass with 328 passed and 2 skipped - [x] My PR passes all required local lint and schema checks - [x] My PR scope is isolated to unscoped managed-file listing and its pagination - [x] I have received a Greptile Confidence Score of at least 4/5, currently 5/5 with no blocking failures at the latest commit ## Delays in PR merge? If review is delayed, I will use the LiteLLM Slack pr-review channel ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Both legs ran the same flow through the real OpenAI Python SDK against a live proxy, with real Postgres and real OpenAI calls, differing only in the commit the proxy booted from. Unified file ids are 200+ characters, so they are aliased `<F1>`..`<F8>` below, oldest upload first. ### Before (3029f7eb844b7e3ba1cc4ca965e162cbd9424d15) #### A caller cannot list files they own Alice uploads 8 managed files, then 3 of them are deleted straight at the provider, bypassing the proxy entirely. She still owns them and the proxy still resolves them by id, but they leave her listing. ``` $ curl -s -X DELETE https://api.openai.com/v1/files/file-1Q9GqDgJ5BkTkHmHrvpLyE -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_KEY' {"object": "file", "deleted": true, "id": "file-1Q9GqDgJ5BkTkHmHrvpLyE"} $ curl -s -X DELETE https://api.openai.com/v1/files/file-CYHEcQqJqx7usYmZxmCaPw -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_KEY' {"object": "file", "deleted": true, "id": "file-CYHEcQqJqx7usYmZxmCaPw"} $ curl -s -X DELETE https://api.openai.com/v1/files/file-7otM9MuGMXyGnY47TjuMWc -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_KEY' {"object": "file", "deleted": true, "id": "file-7otM9MuGMXyGnY47TjuMWc"} $ alice.files.retrieve(<each of the 3 unified ids>) HTTP 200 status='uploaded' (x3) $ alice.files.list() HTTP 200 count = 5 # was 8 a moment ago; nothing changed through the proxy has_more = False decisive file listed? False decisive file listed? False decisive file listed? False ``` Retrieve says the file exists and belongs to her, list says it does not. The only thing that changed is the provider's page. #### `limit` and `after` are ignored, and `has_more` is never true ``` $ alice.files.list(limit=2) HTTP 200 count = 5 # asked for 2, got all 5 has_more = False $ alice.files.list(after="<last_id from the previous page>", limit=2) HTTP 200 count = 5 identical to the previous page = True ``` The next page is byte for byte the previous page, so a paginating client loops forever. Upstream reports `has_more: true` for the same account while the proxy returns `has_more: false` on every response. #### A cursor that cannot exist is accepted ``` $ alice.files.list(after="file-does-not-exist-xyz") HTTP 200 {"data":[ ...5 file objects... ],"has_more":false,"object":"list", ...} ``` ### After (ba64a1c451e1a732f014599348aeea13e1166474) #### The listing is owner scoped and served locally ``` $ alice.files.list() HTTP 200 { "object": "list", "ids": ["<F5>", "<F4>", "<F3>", "<F2>", "<F1>"], "has_more": false, "first_id": "<F5>", "last_id": "<F1>" } equals uploaded reversed (newest first): True ``` Same three provider-side deletions as the before leg, this time against the fixed listing: ``` $ alice.files.list() # unscoped, served from the managed store HTTP 200 count: 8 provider-deleted ids STILL listed: True all 8 owned ids listed: True $ alice.files.list(extra_query={"target_model_names": "my-gpt"}) # scoped, hits the provider HTTP 200 count: 5 provider-deleted ids dropped by the scoped listing: True ``` The unscoped listing keeps them and the untouched scoped path drops them, which is the fix serving ownership from the managed store instead of the provider's page. #### Keyset pagination ``` $ alice.files.list(limit=2) HTTP 200 {"ids": ["<F5>", "<F4>"], "has_more": true, "first_id": "<F5>", "last_id": "<F4>"} $ alice.files.list(after="<F4>", limit=2) HTTP 200 {"ids": ["<F3>", "<F2>"], "has_more": true, "first_id": "<F3>", "last_id": "<F2>"} $ alice.files.list(after="<F2>", limit=2) HTTP 200 {"ids": ["<F1>"], "has_more": false, "first_id": "<F1>", "last_id": "<F1>"} PAGING SUMMARY { "concatenated": ["<F5>", "<F4>", "<F3>", "<F2>", "<F1>"], "has_duplicates": false, "union_equals_uploaded_5": true, "missing": [], "extra": [], "order_matches_single_shot": true } ``` #### Cross-caller isolation, and the cursor is not an id oracle ``` $ bob.files.list() HTTP 200 {"object": "list", "ids": [], "has_more": false, "first_id": null, "last_id": null} LEAK: False $ alice.files.list(after="file-does-not-exist-xyz") HTTP 400 {"error": {"message": "Invalid 'after' cursor: no file found with id 'file-does-not-exist-xyz'.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "after", "code": "400"}} $ bob.files.list(after=<one of ALICE's real unified ids>) HTTP 400 {"error": {"message": "Invalid 'after' cursor: no file found with id '<F1>'.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "after", "code": "400"}} ``` A cursor Bob is not allowed to use and a cursor that does not exist return the same body, so the cursor reveals nothing about another caller's files. #### `limit` bounds match what OpenAI documents ``` $ alice.files.list(limit=0) HTTP 400 {"error": {"message": "Invalid 'limit': integer below minimum value. Expected a value >= 1, but got 0 instead.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "limit", "code": "400"}} $ alice.files.list(limit=-1) HTTP 400 {"error": {"message": "Invalid 'limit': integer below minimum value. Expected a value >= 1, but got -1 instead.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "limit", "code": "400"}} $ alice.files.list(limit=10001) HTTP 400 {"error": {"message": "Invalid 'limit': integer above maximum value. Expected a value <= 10000, but got 10001 instead.", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "limit", "code": "400"}} $ alice.files.list(limit=1) HTTP 200 {"ids": ["<F8>"], "has_more": true} $ alice.files.list(limit=10000) HTTP 200 count: 8, equals all 8 owned: True ``` Because the status is a 400 rather than a 500, the SDK surfaces it instead of retrying: ``` $ OpenAI(..., max_retries=2).files.list(limit=10001) BadRequestError, http_status 400 requests that actually reached the proxy for this one SDK call: 1 ``` #### No regression on the shared list-page helper or the route's other errors `build_list_page` is shared with the managed batches listing, and the route's exception tail was replaced, so both were exercised. ``` $ alice.batches.list() HTTP 200 contains the new batch: True $ alice.batches.list(limit=1) HTTP 200 $ bob.batches.list() HTTP 200 bob sees alice's batch: False $ alice.chat.completions.create(model="my-gpt", ...) HTTP 200 content: "pong" ``` Every other error path out of `GET /v1/files` keeps the status it had before the handler change: ``` no Authorization header -> HTTP 401 auth_error bogus API key -> HTTP 401 token_not_found_in_db target_model_names the key cannot access -> HTTP 403 key_model_access_denied provider=not-a-real-provider -> HTTP 500 internal_server_error (pre-existing, unchanged) limit=abc -> HTTP 422 FastAPI query validation ``` ## Type Bug Fix Test ## Caveats (if any) - `purpose` is filtered after the rows are read, because the managed file table keeps it inside the stored file object rather than in a column. To keep the page contract honest the listing reads successive keyset chunks until it has enough matches to fill the page or the caller's rows run out, so a narrow `purpose` over a large table reads more rows than it returns. That is what guarantees a page is never empty while matches remain, which in turn is what keeps `openai-python` iteration correct, since `SyncCursorPage` takes its next cursor from `data[-1].id` and gives up the moment `data` is empty. Filtering `purpose` in the query itself would need a new column and a migration, which is out of scope here - `/openai/v1/files` does not get this fix. That alias binds `provider="openai"` from the path, so it takes the upstream branch and still lists whatever the provider's page happens to carry. Callers who want the owner-scoped listing have to use `/v1/files` with no provider - `limit` and `after` are still accepted and ignored on the `target_model_names` and explicit-`provider` branches, because nothing downstream can receive them: `file_list` swallows extra kwargs, and the OpenAI, Azure and generic HTTP handlers all stop at `purpose`, with the generic one returning a bare list that has no page shape to hang a cursor on. Threading them through would be a provider-behavior change across every custom provider, so it is deliberately left out. `limit` is still validated on those branches, so an out-of-range value is rejected rather than quietly ignored - Nothing indexes the dominant filter and sort. `LiteLLM_ManagedFileTable` carries `@@index([unified_file_id])` and `@@index([team_id, created_at(sort: Desc)])`, so a service-account key filtering on `team_id` is covered, while a user-keyed caller filtering on `created_by` and an admin reading everything both fall back to a scan and a sort. Keyset pagination bounds what comes back, not what gets scanned. `LiteLLM_ManagedObjectTable` has the same index shape and the shipped managed batch listing already runs this query, so this matches what is already there rather than adding a new pattern - `BaseFileEndpoints.afile_list` changed shape: `user_api_key_dict` is now required and it returns a page dict instead of a list. `_PROXY_LiteLLMManagedFiles` is the only implementation in the repo, the ABC appears nowhere in `docs/`, and `ENTERPRISE_PROXY_HOOKS` is a hardcoded dict so no config can substitute another class. An out-of-tree implementation carrying the old signature would break quietly rather than loudly, since `**data` absorbs the new keyword arguments and the old list shape would be returned as the response body - The `target_model_names` listing still asks the provider and so still depends on upstream state. Fixing that path is deliberately left out of this PR - An unknown `provider` value still returns 500 rather than 400. That predates this PR and is unchanged by it - Live curl proof requires a Postgres-backed enterprise proxy ### Final Attestation - [x] Tests cover owner scoping, purpose filtering, unified IDs, provider bypass, `limit`, `after` paging, `has_more`, a rejected cursor, the documented `limit` bounds on all three route registrations, a page filled past rows the filter drops, a page filled past rows that do not parse, and a filter that matches nothing ### Credit This started as @rimysore's fix for the unscoped listing. The keyset pagination on top of it answers the unbounded result set the review bot flagged and the paging half of #37714

signal.title: ci: ban row-rewriting DML from prisma migrations
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Migrations apply at proxy boot, so row rewrites are downtime - An unbatched `UPDATE` shipped and had to be reverted - Nothing in CI or the conventions stopped it How it solves it: - New code-quality gate rejects `UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE` in migrations - Also rejects `INSERT ... SELECT` and CTE-led rewrites - Escape-hatch marker must name what bounds the rewrite ## User Flow **Before.** Nothing tells the author their migration rewrites rows, and every proxy that picks up the release stops serving while it runs. 1. An engineer adds a migration that backfills a new column with a single `UPDATE` over the spend logs table, and opens a PR 2. They watch the checks on the PR page. Everything goes green, `code-quality` included, and no check says anything about the migration 3. They get an approval and merge, and the change goes out in the next release 4. An operator upgrades to that release and restarts their proxy 5. Their client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions` and gets back `500` with `no_db_connection` 6. `GET https://litellm-domain/health/readiness` keeps failing for as long as the rewrite takes, minutes on a large table, then the proxy starts answering on its own with the table's disk usage roughly doubled **After.** The check names the statement and its line before the migration can merge, so the release boots straight into serving traffic. 1. An engineer adds a migration that backfills a new column with a single `UPDATE` over the spend logs table, and opens a PR 2. Schema changes are cheap and bounded. A statement that touches existing rows is not: its cost scales with the table, and on a spend-log-sized table a single `UPDATE` means minutes of a proxy that is up but not serving, plus a heap that has doubled in size and that plain autovacuum will not hand back. We shipped exactly that and had to revert it, and the part worth fixing is that nothing in the repo said not to, so the next person had no way to know `tests/code_coverage_tests/check_migrations_no_data_rewrites.py` now walks every `migration.sql` under `litellm-proxy-extras` and fails on any statement whose leading keyword is `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE`, on `INSERT` when its rows come from a query rather than a literal `VALUES` list, and on a CTE-led statement wrapping any of those. `INSERT ... VALUES` passes because the literal row list bounds it. The check runs in the existing Code Quality job, which has no path filter, so a migration that arrives through a rebase or a merge is still gated, and it costs nothing extra since that job already runs on every PR Getting this right on real SQL took more than a grep. `ON DELETE CASCADE` and `ON UPDATE CASCADE` appear 60 times across the current migrations and are schema, never a statement's leading keyword, so the checker resolves each statement's own keyword instead of matching anywhere in the text. `DO $$ ... $$` is this repo's idiom for conditional DDL and appears 11 times, so dollar-quoted bodies are scanned recursively and PL/pgSQL block syntax is transparent to the keyword lookup, which also means an `IF EXISTS (...)` guard cannot stand in for the statement it guards. Comments, single-quoted strings, double-quoted identifiers and dollar-quoted bodies are masked in place before parsing, keeping every offset where it was Three things the first pass got wrong, fixed in `7e6d303e38`. Line numbers inside a dollar-quoted body were counted against the sliced body text while the offset into it stayed absolute, so a statement inside a `DO $$ ... $$` block reported a line it does not sit on. Since the escape-hatch markers are matched by line, that same slip cut both ways: an unrelated marker earlier in the file silently exempted a real full-table rewrite, and a marker sitting directly above a bounded one failed to exempt it. Scanning now threads each region's offset through and counts lines against the whole file, however deeply the statement is nested. Second, `EXECUTE 'UPDATE ...'` passed, because the DML sat inside a string literal that masking had already blanked, so the literals an `EXECUTE` runs are now scanned as SQL in their own right; a rewrite reads the same to Postgres whether it is spelled out or handed over as a string. Third, an `INSERT ... VALUES` carrying a scalar subquery in its value list was flagged as an `INSERT ... SELECT`. A top-level `VALUES` bounds the insert to the rows written out there, so the parenthesised subqueries and helper CTEs around it no longer make it a rewrite Two ways round those, closed in `e7dea842c3`. A rewrite can be parked in a variable and run by name a few lines later, where the literal sits outside the `EXECUTE` statement and nothing scanned it, so a literal assigned with `:=` is now read as SQL just like one an `EXECUTE` holds directly. And bounding an insert on the presence of a top-level `VALUES` was too generous, since a `VALUES` reached through a set operation bounds nothing; what decides it now is whether the insert is built on a `SELECT` of its own, which also keeps the scalar subqueries in a `VALUES` list out of it because those sit in parentheses. Both directions err towards flagging, which is the right way to be wrong here: a false positive costs a marker naming the bound, a false negative costs a proxy that boots into a table rewrite Which statement a marker speaks for is its own question, settled in `c4d9a1ac6c`. A marker written on a line of its own speaks for the statement below it, which is how one placed above a rewrite exempts it, and a marker sharing a line with the statement it follows speaks for that statement alone. The old rule looked one line up unconditionally, so writing the marker inline at the end of a statement, a perfectly natural style, quietly exempted the next statement too, and nothing anywhere went red to say so. That was the worst shape a bug in this checker can take, since the whole point of the gate is that a rewrite cannot reach a boot unnoticed Dynamic SQL needed two more corrections, in `622d9c598d`. A marker written above an `EXECUTE` did not reach the SQL that `EXECUTE` runs once the literal's first line sat below it, so the documented placement failed CI and the only way to silence it was to bury the marker inside the string being executed. A marker on an `EXECUTE`, or on the assignment feeding one, now covers what that statement hands off. The other way round, a literal assigned with `:=` was read as SQL whether or not anything ran it, so an error message that happens to begin with the word `UPDATE` was reported as a data migration. A literal now counts only when an `EXECUTE` in the same body runs that variable by name. That direction matters more than it looks: the only way to quiet a false positive is a marker, and a marker on a statement that is not a data migration at all is a lie that erodes what every other marker means One more gap, closed in `3cca3f5402`. `DO` takes its body as a string literal, and dollar quoting is a convenience rather than a requirement, so a migration spelling the body in single quotes got its rewrite through completely untouched. That is ordinary syntax rather than an attempt to hide anything, which makes it reachable by accident, and it is the shape this whole check exists to stop. Quoted `DO` bodies are now scanned like any other SQL a statement hands to the server One last gap, closed in `3d16e327c6`. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the statement it wraps rather than only planning it, so a rewrite underneath one rewrites the table for real on the way to printing its timings. `ANALYZE` is a statement keyword of its own, though, and it sits ahead of the rewrite, so it was being read as the statement's keyword and the rewrite passed. An `EXPLAIN` is now transparent and the statement being explained is what gets judged. The old behaviour was worse than a plain miss, because it had the two cases exactly backwards: `EXPLAIN UPDATE`, which only plans, was flagged, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE`, which runs, was not. Both are flagged now, since nothing here needs the plan of a statement it is being told not to run at boot The last gap, closed in `64267ebd28`, is one this PR introduced itself and is worth tracing because the two halves of it pull in opposite directions. Postgres accepts an insert's row source wrapped in parentheses, so `INSERT INTO "t" ("a") (SELECT ...)` copies a whole table. `777eb8af10` caught that shape by looking for a `SELECT` anywhere in the statement, but that also flagged a scalar subquery sitting in a `VALUES` list. `7e6d303e38` bounded it on a top-level `VALUES`, and `e7dea842c3` replaced that with a `SELECT` read only outside parentheses, which fixed a `VALUES` joined to a query by a set operation and traded the parenthesised form away in the same move. What was missing is that these are two questions rather than one: a query outside every parenthesis is the row source outright, and only when there is none does a top-level `VALUES` get to bound the insert, with a parenthesised query counting when neither applies. All three shapes hold now. `TABLE t` is a row source as much as a `SELECT` is and was passing for the same reason, so it is read as one too, which is safe because double-quoted identifiers are masked before this runs and the bare word can only be syntax. Every form was checked against a live Postgres 16.14 before being called a miss, since a checker gap only matters if the SQL it lets through actually runs `73af0e9692` closes the mirror image of that gap and one next to it. Reading the row source outside parentheses first meant a `VALUES` list still bounded an insert when a set operation joined it to a parenthesised query, so `VALUES (1) UNION ALL (SELECT ...)` copied a whole table with a literal row in front of it. A `VALUES` list now bounds an insert only while no set operation sits beside it at that same level, and a set operation nested inside the list is not beside it, so a subquery with its own `UNION` in it still passes. The second gap is on the dynamic-SQL side: PL/pgSQL parks a string in a variable through a query's `INTO` and through the bare `=` it accepts as the assignment operator, and only `:=` was being read, so a rewrite handed to a later `EXECUTE` went unseen either way. `INTO` is unambiguous and simply counts. A bare `=` is comparison to the rest of SQL, so it names a target only where the words ahead of it are a name and perhaps a type rather than a statement keyword or a word guarding a condition, and those guards stop counting once a `THEN` or an `ELSE` ends the condition they opened. That keeps `IF stmt = 'DELETE FROM ...'` reading as the test it is while catching the assignment written on the same line as the `IF` that opened the block One decision worth naming, since it looks like a gap and is not. A marker on an `EXECUTE` covers a single-quoted payload, because that payload is an opaque string the statement hands to the server. A dollar-quoted payload is not treated as a string at all but as a region read like any other body, so a rewrite inside one carries its own marker, on the rewrite itself, which is also what the failure guidance prints. Making a marker cover a whole dollar-quoted body would read as more consistent and would be a real hole: `DO $$ ... $$` is this repo's idiom for conditional DDL, used by 11 of the 157 migrations on disk, and one marker on the block header would then silence every rewrite inside it, including one added months later by someone who never saw the marker. The current behaviour fails loudly and costs a marker in the right place; the alternative fails silently and costs a proxy booting into a table rewrite. Four tests pin it, and all four fail if the exemption is widened that way Where this stops is written down rather than left to be discovered. Each literal is read on its own, so a keyword assembled by concatenating fragments that do not contain it, `'UPD' || 'ATE ...'`, is not caught. Every fragment is scanned, so a concatenation is caught wherever the keyword survives whole in one of them, which covers `'UPDATE ' || quote_ident(t)` and the rest of the shapes anyone actually writes. Reaching the gap takes a keyword deliberately split down the middle, and this is a guard against a rewrite reaching a boot unnoticed, not a defence against someone hiding one on purpose Two migrations already on disk contain an `UPDATE`. Prisma checksums applied migration files and the repo treats them as immutable, so neither can carry an inline marker. They sit in a closed `GRANDFATHERED` set instead, and the checker fails if either one stops violating or disappears, which keeps the baseline from quietly going vacuous The rule itself is written down in `CLAUDE.md` next to the other conventions, since a gate that fails without explaining the alternative just gets worked around On tests: 124 cases, and I mutation-tested the checker rather than trusting the count. The first pass killed 12 of 18 mutants, and every survivor was a test that named the right feature but picked an input where the feature's absence was masked by the keyword lookup landing on a different, still-harmless keyword. A later commit fixes that, so all 17 killable mutants now die. The eighteenth turned out to be an equivalent mutant: the doubled-quote branch in `skip_quoted` masked the same span whether or not it was there, verified exhaustively over every input up to length 6 in the relevant alphabet, so that branch is gone rather than left as untestable code. The 76 cases added since then cover dynamic SQL, bounded and query-backed inserts, marker placement and its scope inside dollar-quoted regions, quoted `DO` bodies, explained statements, and line numbering under nesting. Run against the earlier checkers, 35 of the 124 fail at `777eb8af10`, 25 at `7e6d303e38`, 29 at `e7dea842c3`, 27 at `c4d9a1ac6c`, 21 at `622d9c598d`, 19 at `3cca3f5402`, 15 at `3d16e327c6`, 15 at `aabaa5151b` and 8 at `64267ebd28`, so they pin real regressions instead of restating what already worked. Two things in that sequence are worth reading. It does not fall monotonically, and the step up at `e7dea842c3` is the parenthesised row source `64267ebd28` closes, with cases that pass at `7e6d303e38` and fail from `e7dea842c3` onwards, which is the suite naming the commit that introduced the gap rather than only the one that fixed it. And `aabaa5151b` ties `3d16e327c6` exactly, which is the same non-behavioural claim its checklist line makes, arrived at from the other direction ## Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR <!-- devin-review-badge-begin --> --- <a href="https://app.devin.ai/review/berriai/litellm/pull/37899" target="_blank"> <picture> <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://static.devin.ai/assets/gh-open-in-devin-review-dark.svg?v=1"> <img src="https://static.devin.ai/assets/gh-open-in-devin-review-light.svg?v=1" alt="Open in Devin Review"> </picture> </a> <!-- devin-review-badge-end --> - [x] c4d9a1ac6c passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 622d9c598d passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 3cca3f5402 passes /live-pr-risk - [x] 3d16e327c6 passes /live-pr-risk - [x] aabaa5151b is non-behavioural against `3d16e327c6`: a docstring, six tests, and one helper reuse, with 0 scan differences across all 157 migrations on disk and all 51 SQL shapes in the suite - [x] 64267ebd28 passes /live-pr-risk. Nothing here is imported by the proxy, so the dependency graph closes inside the one file: the renamed helper has no reference outside it, the suite loads the checker by path rather than by symbol, and the keyword string it reports has no consumer anywhere. signal.title: feat(router): per-group supported reasoning efforts with max and ultra levels
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Effort dropdown offers levels many models reject upstream - Nothing tells a caller which efforts a model group takes - The chat to Responses bridge silently drops max today How it solves it: - Model groups report supported_reasoning_efforts, intersected across deployments - Per-level polarity resolved in one module; xhigh, max, ultra are opt-in - The bridge passes any effort level through to the provider ## User Flow Before: an operator wiring reasoning effort into a model group has no way to see which levels a group takes, so a rejected level only surfaces as a provider error at request time 1. They send GET http://localhost:4000/model_group/info with their key and read the entry for gpt-5.6-sol; nothing in it says which reasoning effort levels the group accepts 2. They open http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=models-and-endpoints, Add Model, Auto Router, and the Reasoning effort dropdown offers the same six levels for every model, gpt-5-mini and gpt-5.6-sol alike 3. They pick max for the gpt-5.6-sol tier and the save succeeds with no warning 4. A request routed to that tier goes out as POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions with `"reasoning_effort": "max"` and comes back 400 `Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'max' with this model. Supported values are: 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'.` 5. They have no way to tell that same level does work on a claude-opus-5 group, so they find out by trying each one After: the group tells the caller exactly which levels it takes, so the level that used to fail upstream is never offered in the first place 1. They send the same GET http://localhost:4000/model_group/info and the gpt-5.6-sol entry now carries `"supported_reasoning_efforts": ["none","low","medium","high","xhigh"]`, gpt-5-mini carries `["minimal","low","medium","high"]`, and a claude-opus-5 group carries all seven up to max 2. Same page, same Add Model flow: gpt-5-mini's dropdown offers Default, minimal, low, medium, high, gpt-5.6-sol offers up to xhigh, and a claude-opus-5 group offers up to max; a group whose deployments intersect to nothing, which one model absent from the model map is enough to cause, keeps the six-level list the dropdown always offered 3. max cannot be picked for the gpt-5.6-sol tier at all, which is the step that used to hand the operator a level the provider then refused 4. A caller who bypasses the picker and sends `"reasoning_effort": "max"` to that group anyway still gets the same provider 400 they got before: the chat-completions gate is unchanged, because litellm converts some chat requests to /v1/responses further down, where max is valid 5. The same level on the claude-opus-5 group still returns 200, and POST http://localhost:4000/v1/responses with `"reasoning": {"effort": "max"}` on gpt-5.6-sol still returns a completed response, so nothing that worked before stops working ## Relevant issues Supersedes #37732, rebuilt on a complete census of every effort-level enumeration site. Design notes: intersection (never any-member) across a group's deployments so routing cannot hand an effort to a deployment that rejects it; polarity mirrors the provider gates (medium/high unconditional, minimal/low opt-out, xhigh/max/ultra opt-in, and none opt-in on azure alone since its gpt-5 config raises without an explicit flag while no other request path refuses the level); gpt-5.6-cyber deliberately gets no effort flags since the map keeps that entry thin, and it carries supports_reasoning true already; the new TypedDict field stays plain like its five siblings, with the repo's writable-ok precedent, because ReadOnly on Pydantic-validated TypedDicts warns; the chat-completions gate keeps owning xhigh alone, since it runs before litellm decides to convert a request to /v1/responses and no map entry asserts the max or ultra flags anyway; deployment model_info is splatted into ModelGroupInfo, so supported_reasoning_efforts validates whatever an operator wrote under that key down to None rather than failing the whole /model_group/info response ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5991 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Two proxies from this repo, one at the merge base and one at the PR tip, on the same config: deployments for `openai/gpt-5-mini`, `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`, `anthropic/claude-opus-5`, `azure/gpt-5-mini`, and `azure/gpt-5.6`, each on live provider credentials. Every call below is a real request against the running proxy with real provider spend, no mocks ### Before (91f2382ab4) #### Group capability advertisement 1. `GET /model_group/info` with the master key 2. No entry carries a `supported_reasoning_efforts` field at all, for any of the five groups #### Chat completions, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 400 litellm.BadRequestError: OpenAIException - Unsupported value: 'reasoning_effort' does not support 'max' with this model. Supported values are: 'none', 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'.` The level reached the provider before anything caught it #### Chat completions, xhigh on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "xhigh"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'` #### Chat completions, max on a claude-opus-5 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'OK'` #### Responses API, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/responses` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": {"effort": "max"}}` 2. `HTTP 200`, `status=completed` #### Anthropic Messages API, max on both groups 1. `POST /v1/messages` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}`, then the same for `gpt-5.6-sol` 2. `HTTP 200` on both. That surface does not carry reasoning_effort, so the level is dropped before any gating and the gpt-5.6 call succeeds even though the same level fails on chat completions ### After (b7717df9da) #### Group capability advertisement 1. `GET /model_group/info` with the master key 2. Every group carries the field, each one the intersection over its deployments: ``` gpt-5-mini ["minimal", "low", "medium", "high"] gpt-5.6-sol ["none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"] opus-5 ["none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max"] azure-gpt-5-mini ["minimal", "low", "medium", "high"] azure-gpt-5.6 ["none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"] ``` #### Chat completions, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 400 litellm.UnsupportedParamsError: reasoning_effort=max is not supported for this model.` Raised at parameter validation, so no provider call is made and the message names the parameter instead of quoting an upstream error #### Chat completions, xhigh on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning_effort": "xhigh"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'`, unchanged #### Chat completions, max on a claude-opus-5 group 1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}` 2. `HTTP 200`, content `'ok'`, unchanged, and the group advertises max as above #### Responses API, max on a gpt-5.6 group 1. `POST /v1/responses` with `{"model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": {"effort": "max"}}` 2. `HTTP 200`, `status=completed`, unchanged #### Anthropic Messages API, max on both groups 1. `POST /v1/messages` with `{"model": "opus-5", "reasoning_effort": "max"}`, then the same for `gpt-5.6-sol` 2. `HTTP 200` on both, unchanged Observations from the run: - /v1/messages ignores reasoning_effort entirely, before and after - gpt-5.6 takes max on /v1/responses, never on chat - Azure gpt-5 refuses none without an explicit map flag - Advertised sets now match every gate the run exercised ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - gpt-5.6 takes max on /v1/responses but not on chat completions - Chat gating stays on xhigh, so max still fails at the provider - A group that intersects to nothing falls back to every level - Unknown effort strings now reach the provider instead of being dropped - ultra is plumbed everywhere but asserted on no map entry - none resolves as opt-in on azure, opt-out on every other provider ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(router): await budget redis pipeline before sync reads
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Router budget sync can replace live spend with an older Redis value - A logging timeout can drop spend already taken off the queue - Virtual-key model budgets crash if the Redis queue lock is missing How it solves it: - Await the Redis increment pipeline before reading spend back - Shield the pipeline and restore the batch if Redis fails or the caller is cancelled - Skip the Redis-to-memory overwrite when the flush did not land - Initialize the same queue lock on the virtual-key model budget limiter ## User Flow Before: a team with a tight provider budget keeps getting completions after spend should have blocked them, and a slow Redis flush plus a logging timeout can let an authenticated client keep spending past the budget 1. The admin sets an openai `budget_limit` of 10 for `1d` on the proxy router 2. Their app sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions until spend should have hit 10 3. The next POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions still returns 200 instead of a budget exceeded error 4. Another authenticated client with the same key can keep sending costly requests while Redis is delayed and continue past the configured budget After: spend stays at the recorded value, later requests are blocked, and a cancelled Redis flush does not drop the spend that already happened 1. The admin sets the same openai `budget_limit` of 10 for `1d` 2. Their app sends the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions until spend hits 10 3. The next POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions returns a budget exceeded error 4. Another authenticated client with the same key cannot ride a logging timeout to spend past the budget ## Relevant issues Fixes #32614 Refs #20886 Backports #20888 onto `litellm_internal_staging` ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This is a Redis/in-memory race, so a single curl cannot show it. The live path is still POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with a provider or virtual-key model budget. The original issue's reproduction is the proof ### Before (669c1334b4) 1. Queue a 60 increment while Redis spend is 100 and in-memory spend is 160 2. Run budget sync while the Redis pipeline is delayed 3. Observed: in-memory spend becomes 100, Redis later becomes 160, later budget checks trust 100 ### After (6498d2f93b) 1. Same queued increment and delayed pipeline 2. Same budget sync 3. Observed: pipeline completes first, Redis and in-memory stay at 160, later budget checks trust 160 A failed or cancelled flush now leaves in-memory at 160 and keeps the 60 increment queued instead of dropping it ## Type Bug Fix Test ## Caveats (if any) - Virtual-key model budget limiter still bypasses the parent initializer, so new queue state has to be set in that subclass too ## Changes This backports the Redis budget sync race fix from #20888 onto `litellm_internal_staging`. `RouterBudgetLimiting` now snapshots and clears the pending Redis increment queue under a lock, awaits `async_increment_pipeline(...)`, shields that write so a logging-worker timeout cannot drop the batch, and skips the Redis-to-memory overwrite if the flush did not land `_PROXY_VirtualKeyModelMaxBudgetLimiter` inherits `RouterBudgetLimiting` but bypasses the parent initializer, so it now initializes the same Redis increment queue lock, flush lock, and detached-batch slot before using the inherited increment path Added router budget regression tests for waiting on the Redis pipeline before sync reads, requeueing failed flushes, keeping in-memory spend when Redis is down, and keeping increments when the flush is cancelled ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat(databricks): add new Claude models and cached token pricing
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Databricks Claude Opus 4.8, Opus 5, Sonnet 5 unpriced, spend logged as $0 - Databricks entries carried no cached token pricing - Databricks cost tracking billed cached tokens at full input rate How it solves it: - Adds the missing Databricks Claude entries with DBU and USD rates - Adds cache write and cache read rates to every Databricks proprietary chat model - Routes Databricks cost tracking through the shared cache aware calculator ## User Flow Before: a team running Databricks hosted Claude with prompt caching sees $0 spend on the newest models, and inflated spend on the older ones 1. They call POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "databricks/databricks-claude-opus-5"` and a cached system prompt 2. The response comes back fine and reports 8000 cache read tokens plus 2000 cache write tokens 3. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and the request is logged at $0 spend, so the model is invisible in cost reporting 4. They repeat the same call against `databricks/databricks-claude-opus-4-6`, which is priced, and the log shows $0.0675 for 11000 prompt and 500 completion tokens 5. That figure charges all 11000 prompt tokens at the full input rate, so caching looks like it saved nothing After: the newest models are priced, and cached tokens bill at Databricks cache rates 1. They call POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "databricks/databricks-claude-opus-5"` and a cached system prompt 2. The response comes back fine and reports 8000 cache read tokens plus 2000 cache write tokens 3. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs now shows that request at $0.034, matching the published Databricks rates 4. They repeat the same call against `databricks/databricks-claude-opus-4-6` and the log shows $0.034 instead of $0.0675 5. The 8000 cached tokens bill at the cache read rate and the 2000 written tokens at the cache write rate, so caching shows up as real savings ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket Resolves LIT-5977 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Rates come from https://www.databricks.com/product/pricing/proprietary-foundation-model-serving at 1 DBU = $0.07, and context windows from https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/foundation-model-apis/supported-models There is no Databricks workspace credential on this machine, so the spend a user would see is captured through the live proxy's own cost endpoint with the exact usage shape Databricks returns for a cached request, rather than by paying for a call A screen recording of the cached request billing through the Admin UI logs page, captured at f5cb5619d0, is posted in the [Slack thread](https://berriaillm.slack.com/archives/C0BE49SAUE6/p1787353730147759?thread_ts=1787353730.147759&cid=C0BE49SAUE6) with the log detail screenshots. The before run below was captured at 66b930b540 and the after run at f5cb5619d0 Shared setup, run once per revision: ```bash cat > /tmp/dbx_config.yaml <<'EOF' model_list: - model_name: dbx-claude-opus-5 litellm_params: model: databricks/databricks-claude-opus-5 api_key: fake-key api_base: https://example.cloud.databricks.com general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 EOF LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config /tmp/dbx_config.yaml --detailed_debug cost() { curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4000/spend/calculate \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"completion_response":{"id":"c1","object":"chat.completion","created":1,"model":"databricks/'"$1"'","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"hi"},"finish_reason":"stop"}],"usage":{"prompt_tokens":11000,"completion_tokens":500,"total_tokens":11500,"cache_creation_input_tokens":2000,"cache_read_input_tokens":8000}}}'; echo; } ``` ### Before (66b930b540) #### newest Claude models 1. `cost databricks-claude-opus-5` -> `{"cost":0.0}` 2. `cost databricks-claude-sonnet-5` -> `{"cost":0.0}` #### cached tokens on an already priced model 1. `cost databricks-claude-opus-4-6` -> `{"cost":0.067500335}` 2. That is all 11000 prompt tokens at $5.00/M plus 500 output tokens at $25.00/M, with the 8000 cache reads and 2000 cache writes charged as fresh input ### After (f5cb5619d0) #### newest Claude models 1. `cost databricks-claude-opus-5` -> `{"cost":0.034000134}` 2. `cost databricks-claude-sonnet-5` -> `{"cost":0.013599866000000002}` #### cached tokens on an already priced model 1. `cost databricks-claude-opus-4-6` -> `{"cost":0.034000134}` 2. That is 1000 fresh input tokens at $5.00/M, 2000 cache writes at $6.25/M, 8000 cache reads at $0.50/M, and 500 output tokens at $25.00/M #### cached tokens end to end through the Admin UI 1. Same 11000 prompt / 500 completion request with 8000 cache reads and 2000 cache writes, driven from the Playground against a mock upstream aliased to `databricks/databricks-claude-opus-5` 2. http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs logs it at `$0.034000`, and the Cost Breakdown itemises Input `$0.00500003`, Prompt Cache Read `$0.00400002` (8,000 tokens), Prompt Cache Write `$0.01250008` (2,000 tokens), Output `$0.01250001` 3. The no cache twin of that request logs `$0.067500`, billing all 11,000 prompt tokens at the input rate ## Type 🆕 New Feature 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Sonnet 5 introductory rates hold through 2026-08-31, then standard rates apply - Cache rates for Gemini and GPT-5 entries follow the same published table - Legacy `dbrx-instruct` and `meta-llama-3.1-70b` aliases point at registry keys that no longer exist, kept as is - The new Claude entries also carry the adaptive thinking, sampling param, and cache minimum flags their Anthropic counterparts already had, which CI enforces - `test_fallback_generalizations` moved its unmapped Databricks id off `databricks-claude-opus-5-1`, which is no longer unmapped now that Opus 5 is in the registry - The UI run used a mock upstream, so the Gemini and GPT-5 Databricks entries were priced through `/spend/calculate` only, not through real provider traffic ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR Link to Devin session: https://app.devin.ai/sessions/564d0e383a354b73b0c83aefa1e814b2

signal.title: fix(complexity-router): retune default tier boundaries to 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.50
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Stock boundaries park technical, multi-part prompts in cheap tiers - Scorer rarely clears 0.35, so COMPLEX is nearly unreachable - Overriding one boundary silently left the other two stale How it solves it: - Retunes shipped defaults to 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.50 - Labelled eval accuracy goes from 28/29 to 29/29 - Missing boundaries now fill from the one canonical default ## User Flow Before: a developer sending a detailed engineering question to an auto router gets the cheapest model back, and the answer is thinner than the question deserves 1. Their admin configures an auto router named `smart-router` with four tiers and no custom score boundaries 2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"model": "smart-router"` and ask a multi-part networking question spanning use cases, performance, and packet loss 3. The reply comes back from the cheapest tier model, visible as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` in the `x-litellm-model-name` response header 4. They send a second request asking for a distributed rate limiter in Python backed by Redis, and it comes back from the second-cheapest tier 5. They open https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs and see both requests billed against the bottom two tiers, so they stop trusting the router and pin a model by hand After: the same two requests reach models that match the question 1. Their admin configures the same auto router, still with no custom score boundaries 2. They send the same multi-part networking question to `"model": "smart-router"` 3. The reply now comes from the mid tier, `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` in `x-litellm-model-name` 4. The rate limiter request now comes from the tier above that, `claude-sonnet-4-6` 5. https://litellm-domain/ui/?page=logs shows both at the tier the prompt warranted, and an admin who preferred the old split can set `tier_boundaries` back to 0.15 / 0.35 / 0.60 ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/<your_test_file>.py -v` - [x] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup, identical on both sides. The auto router deliberately sets no `tier_boundaries`, so it runs on whatever the build ships, and each tier points at a real model through a live gateway ```yaml model_list: - model_name: tier-simple litellm_params: model: openai/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 api_base: https://gateway.litellm-sandbox.ai/v1 api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY - model_name: tier-medium litellm_params: model: openai/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 api_base: https://gateway.litellm-sandbox.ai/v1 api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY - model_name: tier-complex litellm_params: model: openai/claude-sonnet-4-6 api_base: https://gateway.litellm-sandbox.ai/v1 api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY - model_name: tier-reasoning litellm_params: model: openai/claude-sonnet-5 api_base: https://gateway.litellm-sandbox.ai/v1 api_key: os.environ/GW_KEY - model_name: smart-router litellm_params: model: auto_router/complexity_router complexity_router_config: tiers: SIMPLE: tier-simple MEDIUM: tier-medium COMPLEX: tier-complex REASONING: tier-reasoning general_settings: master_key: sk-1234 ``` Both runs boot the proxy the same way, then read back the tier that actually served each request ```bash python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config boundaries_proof.yaml --port 4055 curl -s http://localhost:4055/public/complexity_router/scorer_defaults curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://localhost:4055/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-1234' \ -d '{"model":"smart-router","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"<prompt>"}]}' \ | grep -i 'x-litellm-model-name\|x-litellm-response-cost' ``` ### Before (76d46274c1) #### Shipped boundaries 1. `curl -s http://localhost:4055/public/complexity_router/scorer_defaults` 2. `{'simple_medium': 0.15, 'medium_complex': 0.35, 'complex_reasoning': 0.6}` #### Multi-part networking question 1. Prompt: "Explain the differences between TCP and UDP protocols, including use cases for each, performance implications, and how they handle packet loss in distributed systems" 2. `x-litellm-model-name: openai/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.000115`, so it lands on SIMPLE #### Distributed rate limiter 1. Prompt: "Implement a rate limiter using the token bucket algorithm in Python that supports multiple rate limit tiers and can be used across distributed systems with Redis as the backend" 2. `x-litellm-model-name: openai/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.000357`, so it lands on MEDIUM ### After (3b39ebc093) #### Shipped boundaries 1. `curl -s http://localhost:4055/public/complexity_router/scorer_defaults` 2. `{'simple_medium': 0.1, 'medium_complex': 0.25, 'complex_reasoning': 0.5}` #### Multi-part networking question 1. Same prompt as above 2. `x-litellm-model-name: openai/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.000345`, so it now lands on MEDIUM #### Distributed rate limiter 1. Same prompt as above 2. `x-litellm-model-name: openai/claude-sonnet-4-6`, `x-litellm-response-cost: 0.000357`, so it now lands on COMPLEX Both prompts are labelled COMPLEX in the in-repo eval set, so each moves toward its label. Across that whole set the retune moves 5 of 29 cases up a tier and takes accuracy from 28/29 to 29/29 ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Caveats (if any) - Higher tiers cost more; deployments watching spend should re-baseline - `reasoning_override_min_score` tracks `simple_medium`, so its floor drops too - Labelled eval set is only 29 cases - Old behaviour is one `tier_boundaries` block away ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR
